findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine, so it runs on the event loop thread, but `requests.get` is a synchronous socket call with no yield point. While it waits (up to the 5-second timeout, longer if DNS resolution to `billing.internal` hangs before the timeout applies), no other task on the loop can make progress \u2014 every concurrent request handler is frozen, not just this one. The `async` keyword also makes this invisible at the call site: callers will `await` it and reasonably assume it is non-blocking.

The file already has the right pattern directly above: use `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`, mirroring `fetch_plan` (line 5-7) by taking the client as a parameter so it can be reused. If the synchronous client genuinely must be kept, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the loop stays free.

findings.title: New async function fetch_plan_limits has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs a network call and returns parsed JSON, but no test file is included in this diff. Nothing would catch a regression here — e.g. if the URL template were wrong, the timeout removed, or the response shape changed, no test would fail. Given the existing fetch_plan function above it is similarly simple, this may match existing project standards, but since this is new externally-facing behavior (billing limits used in the UI), at least a basic test mocking the HTTP call and asserting on the parsed return value would catch obvious breakage.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. If `tenant_id` originates from a request path segment, query parameter or JSON body, a caller can inject `/` and `..` segments (e.g. `../../admin/keys`) or a `?`/`#` to reach a different path or append query parameters on the internal, presumably unauthenticated, billing host. The response is then returned to the caller via `response.json()`, making this a readable request-forgery primitive against an internal service.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID / `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) before use, or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Passing it as a parameter rather than splicing it into the path string is safer still.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception type catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is running are converted into a silent `return None`. That makes the process ignore Ctrl-C / shutdown signals that happen to land inside a metrics push, and it can break generator/task cancellation semantics.

Separately, the PR description says "catch and log", but nothing is logged \u2014 every transport failure, serialization bug or `NameError` in `_client` now disappears without a trace, which is exactly the failure mode that makes telemetry outages invisible.

Suggested: `except Exception as exc: logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=exc); return None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently swallows all failures, no log emitted

findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. There is no test verifying that a raising _client.send no longer propagates, nor that a successful send still returns its value. If this try/except were removed or broken, nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.body: The function now silently catches all exceptions and returns None, but there is no docstring, comment, or type hint documenting this behavior change. A caller cannot determine from the function signature or any documentation that a failed push will return None rather than raise an exception, or that the function has become non-fatal by design.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides on line 16, then yields to the event loop on line 18 before writing on line 19 — all outside `_lock`. Two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current` below the limit, both pass the check, and both write, so the tenant is charged past `LIMIT`; with N concurrent callers the overshoot is unbounded. The `await asyncio.sleep(0)` guarantees a suspension point between the check and the write, so this is not a theoretical interleaving.

Additionally, line 19 assigns an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call (which does hold `_lock` and increments) that lands during the `await` has its charge silently overwritten and lost — the rate limiter under-counts as well as over-admits.

Fix: wrap the read, check and write in `async with _lock:` the same way `consume` does, and re-read the counter inside the lock (or increment in place) rather than writing back a value captured before the suspension point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume

findings.title: try_consume's race condition and limit enforcement are untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant, 0) outside of _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) before writing back the incremented value. Concurrent calls can both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check before either writes, allowing the tenant's usage to exceed LIMIT — defeating the purpose of the rate limiter. No test exists (in this diff) that exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, nor even a single-threaded test that LIMIT is actually enforced (e.g. asserting False is returned once the limit is reached, or that _counters does not exceed LIMIT under concurrency). As written, any regression in the limit check or the race itself would go completely undetected.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil; insert failure is swallowed
findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...)` is scoped to the `if` statement and only reaches `log.Printf`. Line 18 then declares a brand-new `var err error`, which is the zero value `nil`, and line 19 returns it. The function therefore returns `nil` unconditionally — a caller that checks `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` can never observe a failed insert, and the end-of-day batch will treat unwritten settlements as committed (no retry, no reconciliation, silent money loss).

Contrast with `WriteEntry` directly above (lines 7-8), which propagates `err` from `db.Exec`. Fix by returning the insert error:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

If "log and continue" really is the intent for the batch, that decision belongs in the caller's loop, and this function should still return the error so the caller can count/report failures. At minimum the signature should not promise an error it never produces.

findings.title: Public function WriteSettlement lacks contract documentation
findings.body: WriteSettlement is an exported public function (capitalized name) whose behavior is contradictory and cannot be safely used without documentation. The function validates input (line 12–14) and returns errors from validation, but then swallows database insertion errors (line 15–17), logs them, and always returns nil (line 19). A caller cannot determine from the signature alone whether this function returns errors or always succeeds. The docstring must clarify: (1) whether validation errors are fatal (they appear to be), (2) whether insertion errors are fatal or merely logged, and (3) whether the function can ever actually return a non-nil error or always returns nil.

There is no test in this diff exercising a failing db.Exec call, so this always-nil-return bug would pass unnoticed. Add a test that forces db.Exec to fail and asserts WriteSettlement returns a non-nil error.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every caller that omits the argument shares the same list object. The first call that has a failing recipient appends to it (line 10) and returns it (line 11); the next call starts from that already-populated list and returns the union of all prior failures plus its own. Callers inspecting the return value to decide what to re-send will re-send recipients from unrelated earlier batches, and the list grows unbounded for the process lifetime.

Use `attempted=None` and build a fresh list inside:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []
    ...
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Mutable default arg accumulates recipients across calls

_Also raised by the security agent:_ send_with_retries does not retry despite its name

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 in a rename-only PR
findings.body:
Every other hunk in this diff is a pure identifier rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes its predicate from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. A remainder of exactly 0.5 now yields 0 instead of 1, i.e. half-cent remainders round down rather than up. Exactly-0.5 remainders are common in money math (half of an odd cent count), so this will change billed totals by one cent on a nontrivial share of lines and will drift any downstream reconciliation against previously stored values.

If this behaviour change is intentional it belongs in its own commit with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary; otherwise restore `>=`.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted silently drops one record per page
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` computes `start = page * PAGE_SIZE` but slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, returning only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. Because the offset still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` on the next page, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — for an export endpoint this means data is lost from the output with no error. Compare the existing `page_of` on line 6, which correctly slices `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`. Change the end bound to `start + PAGE_SIZE`.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single success path at line 16. When the header check fails at line 13 the function returns `None` at line 14 with `fh` still open, and any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) — e.g. a decode error on a non-UTF8 partner file — also escapes with the handle open. findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge — yet `charge_card` is decorated with `@retry(attempts=3)`. A transient failure after the gateway has already accepted the POST (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on the response path) will cause up to two additional charges against the same card. The gateway docstring states it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header; generate a key once per logical charge in `charge_card` and pass it through `charge()` so retries collapse to a single charge, or drop the retry on this path entirely and let the caller reconcile via `get_charge`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge() without Idempotency-Key

findings.title: No test catches duplicate charges from retrying a non-idempotent call

If a transient failure occurs after the gateway processed the charge (e.g., timeout on response), retry() will re-invoke charge() and create a second real charge. There is no test in this diff exercising charge_card's retry behavior, so nothing would fail if this bug is introduced or persists. A test simulating a failure-then-success on charge() and asserting the underlying POST was only invoked once (or that an idempotency key was passed) would catch this.

The wrapper applies automatic retries but carries no docstring warning that the underlying operation is unsafe to retry without an Idempotency-Key header. A caller using `charge_card()` will reasonably expect retries to be safe, but the function silently violates that expectation and risks creating duplicate charges on retry.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

The subtraction on line 10 (`invite.expires_at - cutoff`) between an aware and a naive datetime raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so this function fails unconditionally for every input rather than returning a boolean.

Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. The `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation also silently shifts the comparison by up to one second; drop it unless that rounding is intentional.

Separately, note that once fixed the predicate returns `True` for invites that already expired (negative delta). If callers expect "expires soon but is still valid", they will also need a lower bound.

""`), change the return type to `string | undefined`, or narrow the parameter to a type where `billingContact` is required. findings.title: Removing Referer scrubbing writes auth tokens into the logs
findings.body:
Previously the Referer value was passed through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before being added to the logged header dict; now the raw header value is logged. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, and the browser echoes that full URL — token included — in the Referer header of every subresource request. On any 5xx the token is therefore serialised by `json.dumps(headers)` and written out by `log_method` in cleartext.

Anyone who can read the server log (operators, log shipping/aggregation pipelines, a container stdout collector, a bug report with a pasted traceback) gets a live authentication token for that user's server. Restore the scrubbing for Referer (and consider applying `_scrub_uri` to any other header that may contain a URL) rather than logging the raw value.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Removing _scrub_uri writes auth tokens from Referer into logs

findings.body: The change drops the `_scrub_uri` call that previously redacted the auth token from the Referer header before logging. Per the repository context, `token_authenticated_url` embeds the token directly in URLs, and those URLs are echoed back in the Referer header on subresource requests — meaning this change causes the raw token to be written to logs. There is no test in this PR (or evident in the repo) that asserts logged headers never contain a token/secret value, so this regression would pass unnoticed by the test suite.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL check reintroduces SVG javascript: XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` no longer hits that branch, so it falls through to whatever the generic tail of the function returns. In SVG, `<a xlink:href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">` is a live script-execution sink in browsers that still honour the legacy attribute, and `xlink:href` on `<use>`/`<image>` additionally enables external-reference loading.

The entry point is author-supplied markdown, which the file header states includes end-user submitted content; the sink is the rendered attribute in the DOM. Unless `xlinkhref` is stripped entirely by the allowed-attribute list elsewhere in this function (not shown in the diff), this is an unauthenticated stored-XSS vector.

If the goal is to stop supporting `xlink:href`, drop it from the allowed-attribute list so it is removed from output, rather than removing only its URL validation — the current shape is the worst of the two options: still rendered, no longer checked.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref from the URL check re-enables javascript: XSS

findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` is taken straight from the request query and, with the `common.ValidateID` check deleted, reaches the storage layer unvalidated. `internal/api/database/file/file.go` states explicitly that it "does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point" and then does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. `filepath.Join` cleans the result but does not confine it: a project value such as `../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder`, so the folder-root join does not scope anything on its own. The PR description's premise is therefore incorrect. findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on a value that arrives with the request, before `io.Copy` on line 8 has read (and therefore proven) a single byte. A client that sends `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte body causes the server to reserve gigabytes; a handful of concurrent such requests exhausts the process. The previous behaviour — growing the RW a page at a time as the body was actually read — bounded allocation by bytes genuinely received, which is why it was safe.

If the pre-sizing is worth keeping, clamp it: reserve `min(contentLength, someMaxPartSize)` and only after rejecting `contentLength` values above the configured maximum part size, so allocation is bounded by policy rather than by the header. The MD5/copy loop on line 8 already handles growth correctly for anything beyond the reservation.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) with mismatched/oversized length
findings.body: The new `Reserve(contentLength)` call pre-allocates the multipart RW buffer based on a caller-provided length before any bytes are read. If `contentLength` is inflated relative to the actual body size (or unexpectedly large), this eagerly allocates memory before validation — the same declared-length-allocation risk the PR title names. Nothing in this diff exercises that path: there's no test asserting that a mismatched or oversized contentLength doesn't cause excessive allocation, or that the io.Copy result is still validated against actual bytes read. A regression here (e.g. removing the copy-length check, or an attacker sending a huge Content-Length) would pass silently.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips from https to plaintext http when is_secure unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when the caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case (key absent, i.e. `.get()` returns `None`) fell through to `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats any falsy value — including the missing-key `None` — as insecure, so every request that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` is now downloaded over plaintext HTTP. Since `url` on line 6 is what the S3 request (with its AWS signature/credentials headers) is sent to, this exposes signed requests and object contents on the wire and silently changes behaviour for all existing callers that relied on the secure-by-default contract.

If the intent was only to simplify, preserve the default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure meta is unset

findings.title: Scheme selection logic inverted; default behavior changed
findings.body: The condition has been inverted from `is_secure is False` to `is_secure` (truthy check), which changes the default scheme when `is_secure` is absent or None. Old code: if `is_secure` is absent, defaults to 'https'. New code: if `is_secure` is absent (falsy), defaults to 'http'. This is a breaking change in the public API contract that is not documented as intentional, and any caller relying on the implicit 'https' default will silently switch to 'http' without warning.

findings.title: No test covers the default-scheme flip for unset is_secure
findings.body: The change flips the default scheme from https to http whenever request.meta.get('is_secure') is not explicitly True (e.g. when the key is absent or None), which is a meaningful behavior change from the old logic (only explicit False forced http). No test file is included in this diff, so if this default flip were wrong (e.g. it should default to https for safety), nothing in the current test suite would fail to catch it.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
`request.Method` (fully attacker-controlled, it is the verb on the incoming HTTP request) flows into `action`, which is packed into `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` on line 9 — the value the authorization layer uses to decide whether the caller may act on the repository named by `vars["name"]`. Before this change `http.MethodDelete` produced `action = "delete"`; after it, every method that is not GET/HEAD — including DELETE — produces `"push"`.

The retrieved config documentation states the three actions are distinct on purpose: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." With this change that separation no longer exists at the authn layer: a token or account holding only `push` on a repository can issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and pass the access check, destroying tags/manifests it was never granted delete rights on. This is destructive and silently removes a control that was previously enforced.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (keeping the pull/push branches as they were), so the delete grant is still consulted. If the intent was to simplify, the simplification must still emit three distinct action values.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The diff collapses the method-to-action switch so that DELETE requests now resolve to action 'push' instead of the previously distinct 'delete' action. Per the repository's own documented access model (config.go), pull/push/delete are intentionally distinct so an account can be allowed to push without being allowed to delete. This diff changes that behavior but includes no test file, so a regression (or intentional but incorrect authorization change) that maps DELETE to push would not be caught by any test running with this change.

findings.title: Default action for unlisted methods flips from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The removed `default:` arm assigned `"pull"` to any method not explicitly listed (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, and any non-standard verb). The new condition treats every method other than GET/HEAD as a write, so such requests are now checked against `push`. Read-only clients issuing OPTIONS (e.g. CORS preflight) or any other verb will be rejected where they previously succeeded. If the intent was only to simplify the write branch, keep the explicit method list rather than inverting the default.

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the entry just written to the cache
findings.body:
When `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries, the whole dict is wiped — including `tenant_id`, which was inserted two lines earlier. The caller still gets the correct return value, but the stated purpose of the function ("a live fetch into the shared cache") silently fails for that call: an immediately following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None`. Once the cache is near the limit this also degenerates into repeatedly filling and flushing, so every other caller loses its warm entries too.

Either evict before inserting, or evict a bounded subset (e.g. pop the oldest N keys, or use an LRU such as `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`) so the just-fetched entry survives.

findings.title: A None result from _fetch is cached and is indistinguishable from a miss
findings.body: The return value of `_fetch` is stored unconditionally. If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown or not-yet-provisioned tenant, that `None` is written into `_CACHE`, and `get_tenant` (line 5, `_CACHE.get(tenant_id)`) cannot distinguish "cached negative" from "never looked up" — it will keep returning `None` for that tenant until the cache is cleared. Consider only writing to the cache when `tenant is not None`, or using an explicit sentinel if negative caching is intended.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tenant_id can flush the whole shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` writes an entry for any `tenant_id` it is handed and, once the shared `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries, discards the entire cache rather than evicting a single entry. If this function is reachable (directly or transitively) from a request handler where `tenant_id` is caller-influenced, an attacker can issue ~1000 requests with distinct or nonexistent ids to force `_CACHE.clear()`, dropping every other tenant's cached data and pushing the resulting read load onto `_fetch` and its backing store. Each cycle costs the attacker 1000 cheap requests and costs the system a full cold-cache stampede.

Two cheap mitigations: bound the cache with a per-key eviction policy (e.g. `OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/`cachetools.LRUCache`) instead of `clear()`, and skip caching when `_fetch` returns a falsy/not-found result so unknown ids cannot occupy entries at all.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's fetch/cache/evict logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh performs three distinct behaviours: fetching fresh data via _fetch, writing it into _CACHE, and clearing the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of these are exercised by any test in this diff. If _fetch's return value stopped being cached, or the eviction threshold/logic were broken (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, clearing instead of evicting oldest), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Documentation references renamed flag --workers
findings.body:
The README documents `--workers` as a command-line flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency`. A user following the documentation will use the wrong flag name and the tool will not recognize it, causing their command to fail. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Renaming --workers also renames args.workers, breaking existing readers
findings.body: `add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` changes argparse's derived destination from `workers` to `concurrency`. Any code doing `args.workers` (or `getattr(args, "workers")`) now raises `AttributeError` at runtime rather than failing at import, and any user scripts/CI invoking `--workers` now get `error: unrecognized arguments`. If the intent is only to rename the user-facing flag, keep the destination stable with `dest="workers"`, or add `p.add_argument("--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, help=argparse.SUPPRESS)` as a deprecated alias. Otherwise, update every consumer of `args.workers` in the same change.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. Any caller relying on the docstring will attempt to use the return value as an integer and fail. Update the docstring to describe the new return type and structure.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; docstring and callers unchanged
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer and still documents that contract on line 2 ("Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer"). It now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (`usage > limit`, `usage + n`, `f"{usage} calls"`) will now get a dict and either raise `TypeError` or silently produce a wrong value. Either keep a scalar-returning function and add a separate `daily_usage`, or update every caller and the docstring together. Note also that a dict is falsy when empty whereas `0` was also falsy, so truthiness checks happen to survive while comparisons do not — which makes the breakage easy to miss in a smoke test.

findings.title: Return-type change of monthly_usage has no test covering new shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict of {day: count} instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. If the grouping, key formatting, or aggregation logic is wrong (e.g. wrong SQL grouping, day format mismatch, empty rows), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting the returned dict's structure and values for a known set of calls.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` is a module-level (apparently public) function whose second parameter changed name from `page_size` to `limit`. Positional callers are unaffected, but any caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` — the natural way to call a function with two optional trailing parameters — will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime, not at import. No callers were retrieved for this review, so the impact could not be confirmed.

Either grep for `page_size=` at every call site and update them in this same change, or keep backward compatibility for a release, e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias and map it onto `limit` before calling `_query`.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter as 'page_size'
findings.body: The Args section documents 'page_size' as a parameter, but the function signature on line 1 now uses 'limit'. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name.

findings.title: New request() silently drops verify/cert (and timeout) before send
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` still advertises `verify=None`, `cert=None` and `timeout=None` in its signature, but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` before calling `req.prepare()` / `self.send(prep)`. `verify` and `cert` are never assigned to `req`, never merged with the session `config` defaults, and never passed to `HTTPAdapter.send()` on line 365-366. Entry point: any caller of `Session.request()`/`get()`/`post()` that passes `verify='/path/to/ca.pem'`, `verify=True` or a client `cert=`; sink: the TLS handshake performed inside `adapter.send(request)`. Callers who explicitly ask for certificate verification or present a client certificate get neither, and whatever the adapter's built-in default is silently wins — a MITM on the connection is then undetected. `timeout` is dropped the same way, so a hostile or slow server can hang the caller indefinitely. Either thread these through to `adapter.send()` (e.g. `self.send(prep, verify=..., cert=..., timeout=...)`) or remove them from the signature until the adapter supports them, so the failure is loud rather than silent.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ New `request()` silently drops timeout/verify/cert/prefetch and all session defaults

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the surviving `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or inline the two lines it contained.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter (and pool) is built per request; close() no longer frees it
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request gets its own PoolManager and no connection is ever reused — connection pooling, which `Session` exists for, is gone. Nothing holds a reference to the adapter afterwards, and `close()` is now `pass`, so sockets are only reclaimed by GC. The adapter should be created once (e.g. in `__init__`, honouring `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize`/`support_http0.9` as `init_poolmanager` did) and closed from `close()`.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` inside the package will not resolve
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is explicit-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` only resolves under Python 2 implicit relative imports; under Python 3 (or with `absolute_import` enabled) it raises `ImportError` at import time, making the whole `requests` package unimportable. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Session.send/close rewrite has no accompanying test changes
findings.body: This diff makes substantive behavioral changes: Session.close() becomes a no-op (previously cleared the PoolManager), Session.request() is entirely rewritten to build a Request/PreparedRequest and call self.send(), and Session.send() now delegates to a newly constructed HTTPAdapter() instead of request.send(). No test file is part of this diff, so if HTTPAdapter.send() has a different signature/behavior than PreparedRequest.send(), or if close() silently failing to release pooled connections causes resource leaks, nothing here would fail to alert the team.

findings.title: Stale docstring removed but behavior changed significantly
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it "closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections." This docstring was removed entirely when the method implementation changed from `self.poolmanager.clear()` to `pass`. While removing a docstring for an empty method is not inherently wrong, the removal obscures that the method's behaviour has changed: it no longer performs cleanup that callers might depend on. If this is intentional (cleanup moved to HTTPAdapter), a comment explaining that would prevent confusion.

findings.title: Removal of `init_poolmanager`/`self.poolmanager` breaks documented subclass hook
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` was a public, overridable hook and `session.poolmanager` a publicly reachable attribute; both are removed with no replacement. Subclasses that override `init_poolmanager` will now have their override never called (silently, not loudly), and any code touching `self.poolmanager` — including `close()` before this diff — raises `AttributeError`. If the adapter is taking over pooling, provide an equivalent hook or a deprecation shim.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` can resolve off sys.path
findings.body: This imports a bare top-level name `adapters` rather than the package-local module. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this resolves against `sys.path`, which includes the invoking script's directory — so any `adapters.py` sitting next to the application, or earlier on the path, is loaded and its `HTTPAdapter.send()` becomes the code that performs every HTTP request for this library. That is arbitrary-code substitution on the request path for anyone who can drop a file into the working directory. Use the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, consistent with the other imports in this module (e.g. `from .utils import ...` on line 18).

findings.title: Old request() method renamed to old_request() without docstring update
findings.body: The `old_request()` method at line 172 appears to be the original `request()` method renamed during refactoring. Its docstring (if any) is not visible in the diff, but the name change from a public API (`request`) to what appears to be a deprecated method (`old_request`) should be documented to explain to callers why the method exists and what they should use instead. This prevents confusion about whether `old_request` is part of the public contract.

findings.title: cookies returns None on malformed Cookie header, breaking callers
findings.body:
In the moved property the failure path sets `self._cookies = None` and the property then returns `None`. Both new call sites in `web.py` immediately index it: `if name in self.request.cookies` (line 321) and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (line 367). With a malformed `Cookie:` header this raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` / `AttributeError` instead of degrading gracefully, turning a client-controlled header into a 500 on every request that reads a cookie.

The old code never returned `None` — on a parse error it called `self.clear_all_cookies()` and returned the (possibly partially loaded) `SimpleCookie`. Since `HTTPRequest` has no access to the response, the equivalent here is to reset to an empty `SimpleCookie()` rather than `None`:

```python
except Exception:
    self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()
```

Note this also silently drops the old side effect of emitting clear-cookie headers for a bad cookie jar; if that behaviour matters it has to be re-added on the handler side.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: Public RequestHandler.cookies removed without a compatibility alias
findings.body:
`RequestHandler.cookies` is a documented, public property used by application subclasses and templates (`handler.cookies[...]`). The diff deletes it outright and rewrites only the two in-tree call sites, so any downstream code doing `self.cookies` now gets `AttributeError`. Keep a thin forwarding property on the handler:

```python
@property
def cookies(self):
    return self.request.cookies
```

That preserves the existing contract while the storage moves to `HTTPRequest`.

findings.title: Cookie parsing/exception-handling change has no test coverage
findings.body: The cookies property was moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its exception-handling behavior changed: previously a parse failure called self.clear_all_cookies() (on RequestHandler), now it sets self._cookies = None directly. This changes what get_cookie/clear_all_cookies do when Cookie header parsing fails (e.g. self.request.cookies[name] on a None cookies would raise TypeError instead of the old, if buggy, behavior). No test in this diff exercises cookie parsing, malformed cookie headers, get_cookie, or clear_all_cookies against the moved property, so a regression in this logic would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Comment references old cookies property location
findings.body: The docstring for `clear_all_cookies` states 'Deletes all the cookies the user sent with this request' but no longer reflects that `self.cookies` was the source of truth. While the code correctly updates to `self.request.cookies`, the docstring still implies the old interface. This could mislead maintainers about the cookies property's location.

findings.title: Parameter names not stripped: ` boundary` never matches, breaking uploads
findings.body:
HTTP Content-Type parameters are conventionally separated by `; ` (semicolon plus space), e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryABC` as sent by every mainstream browser and client. `content_type.split(";")` yields `['multipart/form-data', ' boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryABC']`, so `field.partition("=")` gives `k == ' boundary'`, which never equals `'boundary'`. The loop falls through to the `for ... else` branch, logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" and never calls `_parse_mime_body`, so all multipart form fields and file uploads are silently discarded — a regression from the old `'boundary=' in content_type` substring check, which tolerated the space.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider `k.lower()` for case-insensitive parameter names and stripping surrounding double quotes from `v` (`boundary="..."` is legal per RFC 2045).

findings.title: Content-Type parameter matched without strip/case-folding/unquoting
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the RFC-permitted leading whitespace, and `field.partition("=")` is then compared with `k == "boundary"`. For the overwhelmingly common header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----X`, `k` is `" boundary"`, the comparison fails, the `for` loop completes without `break`, and the `else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" — the body is never parsed. RFC 2045 parameter names are also case-insensitive (`BOUNDARY=`) and the value may be quoted (`boundary="----X"`), neither of which is handled, so the value passed to `_parse_mime_body` can carry surrounding quotes and never match the body delimiters.

Beyond the functional breakage, this makes Tornado's view of the request differ from that of any RFC-conformant front-end (WAF, proxy, logging tier): the same header can be "a multipart body" to one and "nothing to parse" to the other, and with a duplicated parameter (`;boundary=A;boundary=B`) this code takes the first while many libraries take the last. Parser differentials like that are the usual foundation for body-inspection bypasses.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, compare `k.lower() == "boundary"`, and strip surrounding double quotes from `v` before passing it to `_parse_mime_body`.

findings.title: New boundary-scanning logic has no test coverage
findings.body: The PR's stated purpose is to fix a bug where 'boundary' isn't the last Content-Type parameter, but no test exercises a Content-Type header with boundary appearing before other parameters (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'). Additionally, the new comparison `k == "boundary"` will fail to match if a field has a leading space after splitting on ';' (a very common real-world format), since `k` is not stripped — this exact regression is unlikely to be caught without a test asserting the boundary is correctly extracted and _parse_mime_body invoked with the right value in these scenarios.

findings.title: get_host() ignores query/fragment, allowing host-parsing confusion
findings.body:
`get_host()` splits off the path on `/` and then treats everything before the first `@` as userinfo, but it never truncates the URL at `?` or `#`. For `http://trusted.example.com?@attacker.com/` there is no `/` before the query, so line 94-95 treats `trusted.example.com?` as userinfo and returns `attacker.com` as the host. `urllib.parse.urlsplit` (and every browser) returns `trusted.example.com` for the same string; `#@attacker.com` behaves the same way.

The consequence is a parser differential: an application that validates a user-supplied or redirect-supplied URL with the stdlib parser and then hands the same string to urllib3 will connect to a host it never approved — a straightforward SSRF / allowlist bypass. Fix by truncating the authority at the first occurrence of `/`, `?` or `#` before looking for `@`, or by delegating to `urlsplit`.

findings.title: No tests accompany new util.py helper functions
findings.body: make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped are newly introduced (moved) into util.py with non-trivial logic (string/list branching, URL parsing with several edge cases like scheme/path/auth/port splitting, and platform-specific poll/select behavior) but no test file is included in this diff. If get_host mis-parses a URL with an unusual combination of '@', ':' and '/' (e.g., a path containing '@' after credentials), or if make_headers mishandles a non-str/non-list accept_encoding value, nothing in this change would catch the regression.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` passes a format string with no argument, so the raised exception literally reads `Failed to parse: %s` and callers/log readers lose the only diagnostic that matters — which URL failed. Should be `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or `% port`, whichever the original reported).

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode value is silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The type test uses the bare builtin `str`. Under Python 2 a `unicode` value (very common, e.g. from a config file or a `from __future__ import unicode_literals` caller) is neither `str` nor `list`, so it falls into the `else` branch and the caller's explicit encoding is silently discarded and replaced by `'gzip,deflate'` — a wrong header with no error. Since `six` is already imported in this module, use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)`.

findings.title: "status" sort key is never exercised by a test
findings.body: SORTABLE maps three keys (created_at, amount, status) to real column names. Tests cover created_at (default) and amount (ascending), but no test calls list_invoices with sort="status", so a typo or wrong mapping for that column (e.g. mapping to a nonexistent column, or the wrong direction) would not be caught.

findings.title: New test file uses discount_for, Customer and Decimal with no imports
findings.body: The hunk header `@@ -0,0 +1,6 @@` covers the whole newly added file, and none of the six lines import `discount_for`, `Customer`, or `Decimal`. As written the module raises `NameError` at test execution, so neither test actually exercises the extracted helper. Add `from decimal import Decimal` and the imports for `discount_for` and the `Customer` model (or a fixture/stub providing `.tier`). If these names arrive via a `conftest.py` star-import or plugin, this is a non-issue.

findings.title: `self.location` now a URL object, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument, so it was whatever the caller passed (typically a `str`). After this change it is a `yarl.URL` instance. The documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that application code "compares it against configured strings and passes it to ``str.startswith``". `URL` has no `startswith` method, so existing callers will raise `AttributeError`, and equality comparisons against plain strings (`exc.location == "/login"`) will now silently evaluate to `False`. Additionally `URL` normalises/percent-encodes input, so even `str(exc.location)` may not round-trip to the original argument.

Keep the original value on the attribute and use a local for the header:

```python
self.location = location
self.headers['Location'] = str(URL(location))
```

If exposing a `URL` is the intent, it needs a separate attribute plus a documentation and changelog entry, since it is a breaking public-API change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `location` type change can silently break redirect-target checks

findings.title: Location attribute now violates its documented contract
findings.body: The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object (line 8) instead of the original string value. However, the documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it should be 'the string it was constructed with', and describes application code comparing it against configured strings and passing it to `str.startswith`. Application code relying on this documented contract will break when receiving a `URL` object instead of a string.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented string type
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string. Per docs/web_reference.rst, application code relies on `.location` being 'the string it was constructed with' and calls str.startswith on it. Since URL doesn't support startswith the same way a str does, this is a behavior-changing regression. Nothing in this diff (no test file present) asserts the type or value of `self.location` after construction, so this change could silently break callers that treat it as a string.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, "which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was exactly that re-check. With `if`, a single spurious wake falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8 with an empty buffer and `self._eof` still false, so `readany()` returns `b""` even though the stream has not ended. Callers conventionally treat an empty return from `readany()` as EOF and will terminate their read loops early, silently truncating the body. Restore the `while` so the condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single-wait read can return empty bytes, signalling a false EOF

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wakeup re-check behavior for readany
findings.body: The change replaces a `while` loop with a single `if`, which changes behavior when `_wait` resolves without new data arriving (a documented possibility per the docstring: "waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer"). Previously the loop would re-check and wait again; now it proceeds directly to `_read_nowait(-1)` after one wake, potentially returning an empty/incomplete read prematurely. There is no test in this diff exercising a spurious wakeup with an empty buffer and `eof` still False, so this behavior change would not be caught by any existing or new test.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body:
`requests/adapters` is a submodule of the `requests` package, not a top-level module. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path` only and raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time — meaning `import requests` fails outright for every consumer. Even on Python 2 it only works by accident and would break the moment `absolute_import` is enabled. Worse, if any unrelated top-level `adapters` module happens to be installed, the wrong `HTTPAdapter` would be bound silently. Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Import change alters module resolution semantics

findings.title: Unqualified `adapters` import is resolvable from sys.path (module hijack)
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` binds unambiguously to the module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is resolved through `sys.path`, which normally begins with the invoking script's directory (or `''` — the current working directory — for `-c`, `-m` and interactive use). Any `adapters.py` or `adapters/` package sitting in that directory, or in any earlier `sys.path`/`PYTHONPATH` entry, will be imported instead, and its module-level code runs with the full privileges of the process the moment `requests.sessions` is imported.

The hijacked name is not incidental: `HTTPAdapter` is what constructs the pool manager and therefore controls certificate verification and proxying for every request the session makes. A substituted class can silently disable TLS verification or redirect traffic, with no error surfaced to the caller.

Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. If the goal was to modernise the import style, the safe modernisation is the fully-qualified absolute form `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`, not the bare name.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see tornado/httpserver.py, which returns `None` explicitly from the property). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`. This turns a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 on any handler that calls `get_cookie` — an unauthenticated remote trigger. The PR premise that "cookies is always a mapping after construction" is contradicted by the property itself. Restore the `is not None` check, or change the property to return an empty mapping and update all consumers together.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection for standard Content-Type headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the surrounding whitespace on each parameter. For the canonical header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX`, the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"`, so `partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` comparison on line 5. The loop then ends without ever calling `_parse_mime_body`, so multipart bodies are silently discarded: no form arguments, no uploaded files, and no error raised to the caller. The strip was not redundant — it is what normalises the split output. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and keep stripping the value, since a trailing `\r`/space or a quoted boundary would otherwise be passed through verbatim to `_parse_mime_body`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Dropping strip() on Content-Type params breaks/skews boundary parsing

findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partition, meaning a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (with a leading space before 'boundary') will now produce k == ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', causing the boundary detection at line 5 to silently fail to match. No test in this diff (or evidently in the surrounding repo, since none was retrieved) exercises this parsing path with whitespace-separated Content-Type parameters, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Format string placeholder has no argument
findings.body: The error message on line 7 contains the format placeholder `%s` but does not provide an argument to fill it. This will cause a `TypeError` at runtime when the exception is raised, rather than displaying the intended error message with the URL that failed to parse. The placeholder suggests the original intent was to include the problematic URL in the error message for debugging purposes.

findings.title: No test covers LocationParseError message content

No test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) asserts on the exception message text for this code path, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message after removing `% url`
findings.body: The interpolation argument `% url` was removed but the `%s` placeholder remains, so the exception message is the literal string `Failed to parse: %s`. Anyone reading the traceback or logging `str(exc)` loses the URL that failed to parse, and the dangling `%s` looks like a formatting bug to the reader. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or `LocationParseError("Failed to parse URL")`); if the URL should stay, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string interpolation into shell=True command
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by interpolating `name` and `directory` directly into a string that is then run with `shell=True`. Two concrete failures follow:

1. Correctness: a `directory` of `my photos` is word-split into two tar operands, so tar archives `my` and `photos` (or fails); a `directory` containing `*` or `?` is glob-expanded by the shell, silently archiving a different set of paths than requested.
2. Security: a `name` of `x; rm -rf /exports` or `$(...)` executes arbitrary commands, because nothing sanitises either argument.

Build an argument list instead and drop `shell=True`:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

and validate that `name` cannot contain `/` or `..` so the output path stays inside `/exports`. This also matches the list-form call already used by `list_exports` on line 5.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shell injection: unsanitised name/directory interpolated into shell=True

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command by interpolating `name` and `directory` directly into a string executed with shell=True.
