At minimum a test verifying the exact command string built for given inputs (and that special characters are rejected or escaped) would catch regressions here.

findings.title: Return shape inconsistent with sibling list_exports
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess`. Callers of this module will have to remember which one unwraps. Either return the `CompletedProcess` from both, or return something meaningful here (e.g. the archive path `f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz"`) so the function's result is usable without inspecting subprocess internals.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` widens the origin allowlist from the curated `ALLOWED` list (line 6) to `"*"` while keeping `credentials: true`. Any route this middleware is mounted on will accept cross-origin requests from every origin on the internet and instruct the browser to attach the user's cookies/authorization headers, letting any attacker-controlled page read authenticated responses on behalf of a logged-in victim.

Note on exact behaviour: the express `cors` package emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for `origin: "*"`, and browsers refuse to honour a literal `*` on credentialed requests — so as written the dashboard will *not* work, which strongly suggests the next commit will "fix" it by reflecting `req.headers.origin`, which is the fully exploitable form. Either way this should not land.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin (or add it to `ALLOWED`) rather than `"*"`, e.g. `origin: ["https://dashboard.example.com"], credentials: true`. If a genuinely public, unauthenticated surface is needed, keep `origin: "*"` but set `credentials: false`.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body: `cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the middleware emit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch/CORS spec forbids this pairing: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`), the browser treats a literal `*` in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` as a mismatch and fails the request, so the dashboard's cookie-bearing calls will be blocked rather than allowed. The PR's stated goal is therefore not met by this configuration. Reflect the specific dashboard origin instead — e.g. add it to the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6, or pass a function/array containing the exact dashboard origin — so a concrete origin value is echoed back alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

findings.title: No test exercises dashboardCors behavior
findings.body: The new dashboardCors export sets origin: "*" together with credentials: true, which is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers refuse wildcard origin with credentialed requests) and likely won't work as intended for the dashboard. There is no test verifying the actual response headers or the cross-origin credentialed request behavior, so this misconfiguration would ship silently and only surface as a runtime failure in the browser.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to the repository, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key` in `client()`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a sandbox one. Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who obtains a clone, a CI artifact, a container image layer, or the git history after a later removal — can issue charges and refunds against the production payments account.

Actions: (1) revoke and rotate this key at AcmePay immediately, assuming it is already compromised; (2) restore the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` removal on line 1 must be reverted too); (3) purge the value from git history, since deleting it in a follow-up commit leaves it recoverable.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Hardcoded live secret key in source code

findings.title: Env-based key replaced by a baked-in live key for every environment
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing one failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the module-level constant `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is the only source, and its value is prefixed `acme_live_`. Every environment that imports this module — including test runs and staging — will now transact against the live payments account, and there is no override hook left. Restore the environment lookup (or take the key as a parameter with an env-var default) so non-production deployments cannot charge real cards, and rotate the key that was committed.

findings.title: No test exercises client() to verify api_key wiring
findings.body: The PR adds only a fixture (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) that returns a fake dict; there is no actual test that calls billing/acmepay_client.py's client() and asserts acmepay.api_key was set as expected. As written, any regression in how the key is wired up (e.g. reverting to env var, using the wrong constant, or breaking the assignment) would not be caught by anything in this diff.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module object (after setting `api_key` on it), but `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`. Any test that substitutes `fake_client` for `client` will get an object with no `acmepay` methods, so the fixture can only ever assert on the key and will fail as soon as a test exercises a charge call. Make the fixture return a stub object exposing the same attributes/methods the production code calls.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, attacker-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a token body that no one has authenticated. Anyone who can reach an endpoint that calls this can forge a payload naming any tenant and get that value back; the decoder will happily parse a token with a garbage or absent signature. Sitting two lines below `claims_for`, which does verify with `public_key()` and pins RS256, this reads as an intentional shortcut to avoid the key-store round-trip — but the saving is the entire authentication check for tenant scoping.

If the goal is to avoid re-fetching the key per call, cache `public_key()` (or the verified claims) rather than skipping verification: `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If there is a genuine need for pre-verification inspection (e.g. picking a key by `iss`), the function should be named and documented to make clear its result must never be used for authorization decisions, and the tenant used for scoping must still come from the verified path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: New unverified-token tenant extraction has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() is a new function that decodes JWTs with signature verification disabled and returns a claim used presumably for tenant routing/authorization. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing exercises this function — a malformed token, a missing 'tenant_id' claim (KeyError), or someone accidentally reusing this function in a security-sensitive path would go unnoticed. Since this changes trust behavior (verified vs unverified decode), at minimum a test verifying it extracts tenant_id from an unsigned/unverified token and a test for the missing-claim error case should be added.

findings.title: Unchecked dict access raises KeyError when tenant_id is absent
findings.body: With verification off, any syntactically valid JWT decodes successfully, including one whose payload has no `tenant_id`. Line 12 indexes the dict directly, so such a token produces an uncaught `KeyError` rather than an auth-style failure — likely surfacing as a 500 at the request boundary instead of a 401/403. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` and have the caller handle `None`, or raise an explicit auth error here.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it before `pm.save()` (lines 13-14) — with no authorisation check. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates; its result is bound to `user` and never used, which is itself the tell that the check was dropped. The read handler immediately above does the right thing: line 6 calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` before returning data, and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this."

Impact: any authenticated user who enumerates or guesses a `pm_id` can rewrite the billing name on another account's stored card — an IDOR on a payment object, which also sets up downstream fraud/chargeback-dispute confusion.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any mutation. Consider also validating that `body` contains `billing_name` rather than indexing it directly, so a malformed request yields a 400 rather than an unhandled `KeyError`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed request

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, including missing ownership check
findings.body: update_payment_method fetches a PaymentMethod and mutates it without calling require_owner (unlike get_payment_method just above it, which does). No test exists that would catch a non-owner successfully updating another user's payment method, nor one verifying the update behaves correctly for the owner. Since this is a behavior change with no accompanying test, a broken or missing authorization check would go completely unnoticed.

findings.title: Public endpoint missing authorization documentation
findings.body: The new `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint that updates a user's saved payment method, but lacks any docstring describing its authorization contract. Looking at the repository conventions in `api/auth.py`, every object mutation must call `require_owner()` to verify the user owns the object they are modifying. The code on lines 11-14 does not call `require_owner()` before allowing the update, and there is no documentation explaining what authorization (if any) is enforced. A caller reading this function signature would not know whether the authorization check is missing or simply not documented.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint left with no request throttling
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point: an attacker fully controls the `email` argument and it flows directly into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no counter, cooldown or captcha in between. Removing `@rate_limit("5/hour")` makes this a free mail-sending primitive — an attacker can flood any chosen address (reset-bombing / harassment), burn the sending domain's reputation and quota, and if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, enumerate accounts at unlimited speed. It also lifts the ceiling on how many valid reset tokens can be minted for one account in a short window, which weakens any token that is short-lived-but-guessable.

The justification that "the email provider already throttles" does not cover this: provider-side throttling is typically per-sender/global, so it protects the provider's queue, not the victim's inbox, and when it trips it degrades reset delivery for every legitimate user — a denial of service rather than a mitigation. It also does nothing for the enumeration and token-minting effects, which happen before any mail is handed off.

Keep a per-IP *and* per-target-email limiter on this handler, or move the equivalent limit into middleware and reference it here so the protection is visible at the endpoint.

findings.title: Provider throttling is not equivalent to the removed per-caller limiter
findings.body: The decorator was the only request-rate control in this function, and the justification ("the email provider already throttles") substitutes a control with different semantics. A provider-side throttle is keyed on the sending account or destination address and is enforced *after* `send_reset_email` is invoked, whereas `@rate_limit("5/hour")` bounded the number of calls reaching this handler. Concretely, after this change the body still returns `{"sent": True}` unconditionally on line 3 without inspecting the result of `send_reset_email` on line 2, so once the provider starts rejecting or queueing traffic the handler keeps reporting success and the failure is invisible to the caller. If the intent really is to rely on provider throttling, the handler needs to propagate the provider's rejection (return a non-success shape or raise) rather than reporting `sent: True` for mail that was never accepted; otherwise the limiter should stay.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing/removing rate limiting on reset endpoint
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`. There is no test file in this change, so nothing would fail if this removal were wrong (e.g. if the email provider's throttling assumption is incorrect or absent). A test asserting that repeated calls to `request_reset` are throttled (or explicitly documenting that throttling is now delegated to the email provider) would catch a future regression or validate the current change.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path escape
findings.body:
`read_export` resolves the requested name through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead does a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` (line 20). `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/shadow` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the preview endpoint returns the first `limit` bytes of any file the process can read. Since the PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download", the fix is to reuse the same guard: `path = _confined(name)` and then `fh.read(limit)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path bypasses _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: No test covers path confinement for new preview function
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which routes through _confined(name). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if 'name' contained a traversal sequence like '../../etc/passwd' and the function read outside EXPORT_ROOT. Since this is a new function with different path-handling behavior than its neighbor, a test asserting that traversal attempts are rejected (or that the resolved path stays under EXPORT_ROOT) would catch a regression here; none exists.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes `report_ids` (caller-supplied) and fetches each `Report` by ID, then serialises all of them into the response. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced `obj.tenant_id == user.tenant_id` has been deleted, and `require_owner` is no longer even imported. Authentication via `current_user(request)` still happens, but authentication is not authorisation — any authenticated user of any tenant can now enumerate or guess report IDs and read another tenant's report contents in bulk.

Restore the check. If the loop was a performance problem, do the authorisation in the data layer instead of dropping it, e.g. fetch with a tenant predicate (`Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and 403/404 on any ID that does not come back, so the cost is one query rather than N checks.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership

findings.title: bulk_export public API contract undocumented after authz removal
findings.body: The bulk_export function is a public endpoint that previously enforced per-object authorization via require_owner(). The diff removes this check with the rationale that "callers are already authenticated," but this critical behavioral change is not documented anywhere in the function. Callers cannot know from reading the function signature or any docstring whether they are responsible for authorization or whether the function performs it. This is a public API contract defect: a competent caller could reasonably assume the function still validates ownership, especially given that the imported require_owner function exists and is documented as mandatory ("Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this"). Either restore the authorization check or add a clear docstring explaining why it is the caller's responsibility.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both values are single-quoted inside the statement, so a caller value containing a `'` terminates the literal and the rest is parsed as SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` or a `UNION SELECT` against other tables is equally reachable depending on driver multi-statement settings.

Per the PR description these arguments come from a support-facing name/status search endpoint, so they are request-supplied. Fix by keeping the LIKE wildcards in the parameter value rather than the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

This matches `get_customer` on line 5 and satisfies `execute`'s documented contract that "`params` must carry every caller value".

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s required params channel
findings.body:
`execute(sql, params=None)` in `billing/db.py` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is a plain correctness defect for benign input: a customer name such as `O'Brien` closes the quoted literal and the statement fails with a syntax error (or silently matches the wrong rows). Any `%` or `_` a user types also becomes a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal.

Fix by keeping the value out of the SQL text:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

findings.title: Public function lacks contract documentation for parameterized queries
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is a public query function in the same module as `get_customer`, which is documented with the constraint that "params must carry every caller value" (see billing/db.py line 6). The new function does not document its contract, leaving callers unaware of the requirement to pass values through the `params` argument of `execute()`. The function signature does not make clear whether the parameters are safe to pass directly, creating a risk that callers will use it unsafely.

findings.title: search_customers has no test covering its SQL construction
findings.body: search_customers builds its query via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text, bypassing the execute() helper's parameterisation contract used by get_customer. There is no test exercising this function, so nothing would fail if the query were malformed, if special characters in `term`/`status` broke the LIKE clause, or if the interpolation behaved incorrectly. Add a test that calls search_customers with representative values (including quotes/wildcards) and asserts on the SQL/params passed to execute.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by send_webhook
findings.body:
The existing send path validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before issuing `requests.post`. The new `verify_endpoint` takes a tenant-supplied URL and issues `requests.get` straight away with no host parsing and no allowlist check, so a tenant can point it at internal addresses (`http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:…`) and learn the response status — and, because `requests` follows redirects by default, an allowlisted host could redirect into the internal network too.

Apply the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` membership test used on lines 8-9 before the request, and consider `allow_redirects=False` so the check cannot be sidestepped by a redirect.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS SSRF allowlist

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test and lacks host validation present elsewhere
findings.body: verify_endpoint() is new, unauthenticated-looking code that issues an outbound GET to an arbitrary URL, but unlike the existing send function it does not check the host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before making the request. No test exists for this function, so if it were changed to remove timeout, change status handling, or introduced regression, nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code will most plausibly be called to decide whether a tenant's URL is usable. But `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout` or `InvalidURL` for exactly the inputs verification is meant to reject — an unreachable host, a slow host, a malformed URL — so those cases surface as an uncaught exception rather than a failure result. Wrap the call and return a sentinel (or `None`) on `requests.RequestException`, or document that callers must handle it.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is a public API (not prefixed with `_`) that returns a status code without documenting what constitutes a successful verification. Callers cannot determine from the signature alone whether they should check `== 200`, `< 400`, or some other condition. This creates risk of misuse.

findings.title: New customer-invoices bucket has all S3 public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is created alongside an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`: `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, and `restrict_public_buckets`. This is the account-level safety net that stops any bucket policy or object ACL from making customer invoices world-readable; with it off, a single subsequent policy change, a misconfigured upload with `public-read`, or a compromised CI role with `s3:PutBucketPolicy` immediately exposes customer financial documents to anonymous internet readers. No bucket policy is visible in this diff, so I cannot confirm the data is public *today* \u2014 but the control that would have prevented it is explicitly switched off.

Unless this bucket is genuinely meant to serve invoices to anonymous users (it almost certainly is not, given the name), set all four fields to `true`, or simply omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` override so the account-level block applies.

Separately: the PR description says this change adds "the public assets bucket for the marketing site". The invoices bucket is not mentioned and appears to be outside the stated scope \u2014 worth confirming it was intentional before merge.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket added with all public-access protections disabled

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function is untested
findings.body: verify_acmepay is added with no test in this diff. Nothing exercises it to confirm it correctly validates a matching signature or rejects a mismatched one, and no test would catch the difference in comparison behavior versus verify_stripe (== vs hmac.compare_digest). findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but its body contains no `await` — it calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the calling thread. Because the coroutine runs on the event loop, every other in-flight request handler is frozen for the duration of the HTTP call: up to the 5s timeout on read, plus DNS and connect time which `timeout=5` as a single float also covers but does not bound per-phase in the way callers may assume. Under any concurrency this converts a slow billing backend into a full-service stall.

Use the async client already imported in this module, mirroring `fetch_plan` on line 5, e.g. accept or create an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`. If the synchronous call must be kept, wrap it with `asyncio.to_thread(...)` (or `run_in_executor`) so the loop stays free, and drop the `requests` import added on line 2 if it becomes unnecessary.

findings.title: Async function name misleads about blocking I/O
findings.body: The function `fetch_plan_limits` is defined as `async` but performs a synchronous blocking network call via `requests.get()`. Callers seeing an `async def` will expect non-blocking I/O and may incorrectly use this function in tight async loops or critical paths, causing event loop stalls. Either rename to clarify it is blocking (e.g., `fetch_plan_limits_blocking`), remove `async`, or replace `requests` with `httpx` to match the async pattern established by `fetch_plan` on line 5.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is formatted directly into `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}` with no encoding or validation. If `tenant_id` is caller-influenced (e.g. taken from a request path, query string or JSON body), a value containing `../` or a URL-significant character lets the caller steer the request to other paths on the internal billing host — an internal service that is presumably not reachable from outside and may treat any caller as trusted. `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a crafted path landing on a redirecting endpoint can move the request elsewhere.

Fix by validating the identifier against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, and/or percent-encoding it with `urllib.parse.quote(tenant_id, safe='')`. Passing it as a query parameter (`params={...}`) rather than splicing into the path also removes the path-traversal surface. Consider `allow_redirects=False` for an internal RPC-style call.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits' async/blocking behaviour
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous requests.get call inside it, which will block the event loop. No test exercises this function at all, so this regression (or any future breakage of its JSON-parsing/error behaviour) would go unnoticed. At minimum, add a test that calls fetch_plan_limits (mocking requests.get) and asserts on the returned value, and ideally a test that would fail if the call blocked the loop (e.g. running concurrently with another coroutine).

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of silent failure behavior
findings.body: The `push_metrics` function is now a public API that catches all exceptions and returns `None` on failure. Callers need to know that this function will not raise an exception and may silently fail. Without documentation, callers may assume the function either succeeds or raises an error, leading to incorrect error handling. Add a docstring documenting the return value semantics and exception behavior.

findings.title: try_consume checks and writes the counter without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then yields to the event loop on line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 using the value captured *before* the suspension. Two consequences, both reachable with ordinary concurrent traffic:

1. Limit bypass: N coroutines can each read a `current` below `LIMIT`, all pass the check on line 16, and all commit their cost. The effective ceiling becomes `LIMIT + (N-1)*cost` rather than `LIMIT`, which defeats the stated purpose of stopping a noisy tenant from starving others.
2. Lost update: line 19 assigns an absolute value rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` (line 10) or other `try_consume` that committed during the suspension is erased, so accounting drifts downward and the limiter under-counts permanently.

Fix by wrapping the whole read-check-write in the existing lock and re-reading inside it, e.g. `async with _lock:` around lines 15-20, with the counter read after the lock is acquired and no `await` on anything else between the check and the write. Note that `consume()` already takes `_lock` for the same dict, so as written the two functions do not mutually exclude at all.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act without the lock in try_consume

findings.title: No concurrency test for try_consume's check-then-act race

With no test in this diff exercising concurrent calls to try_consume, two tenants' requests interleaved around the await could both pass the LIMIT check and push the counter above LIMIT, and nothing here would fail to reveal it.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding failed settlement inserts
findings.body:
The `db.Exec` error is bound inside the `if` statement's scope, logged, and then discarded. Lines 18-19 declare a brand-new `err` that is never assigned, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` unconditionally — including when the INSERT failed or the connection was down. The signature advertises `error`, so the end-of-day batch caller will treat a dropped settlement row as a successful write, and the discrepancy only surfaces at reconciliation. Note the contrast with `WriteEntry` directly above (line 8), which propagates its `Exec` error.

If the intent really is "log and continue per row", that decision belongs to the caller iterating the batch, not to this function: return the error here and let the loop log-and-continue. Otherwise change this to:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
	log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
	return err
}
return nil
```

and delete the dead `var err error`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Settlement insert failure is swallowed and reported as success

findings.title: Public function behavior contradicts its contract
findings.body: WriteSettlement's signature promises to return an error indicating success or failure. However, the implementation swallows the database error on line 15-17 (logging it but not returning it) and always returns nil on line 19. Callers expecting standard error semantics—where a non-nil return means the operation failed—will be misled and continue processing as if the settlement insert succeeded when it actually failed. This is a contract violation that will cause silent data loss in production. Either remove the exported status, document the swallowing behavior with an explicit comment, or fix the return value to match the caller's reasonable expectation.

findings.title: Retry wrapped around non-idempotent charge can double-charge
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that happens *after* the gateway has recorded the charge (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx from a proxy in front of a succeeded POST) will be retried and create a second and third charge. The retry decorator cannot distinguish "request never arrived" from "response never came back".

The gateway docstring already names the fix: pass an Idempotency-Key header so the gateway collapses the repeats. Generate one key per logical charge *outside* the retry loop (e.g. `charge_card` accepts or derives an `idempotency_key` and passes it through to `charge`), so all three attempts share the same key. Without that, remove the retry from this path and let the caller decide.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat", so the retry there is correct. Only the new path is unsafe.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Non-idempotent charge call wrapped in retry without safety docs

The gateway requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe, but this requirement is not documented in `charge_card`. A caller using this function without passing an Idempotency-Key will create multiple charges on retry, causing financial loss. Add a docstring explaining the idempotency requirement and how to satisfy it.

findings.title: New retrying charge_card() wrapper has no test guarding against duplicate charges

Applying @retry(attempts=3) to it means a transient failure after the gateway already processed the charge will cause up to 3 real charges. findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every input. findings.title: Referer is logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
`_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` was the only thing stripping the `token` query parameter out of the `Referer` header before it reached the log. `token_authenticated_url` builds notebook URLs as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and browsers echo that full URL back in `Referer` on every subresource request — so after this change any 5xx writes a live authentication token into the log stream in cleartext. Anyone who can read logs (ops tooling, log shipping, a support bundle attached to an issue) can replay it and authenticate as that user. Restore the scrub for the `Referer` header; if the goal was just to simplify, keep the special case:

```python
value = request.headers[header]
if header == "Referer":
    value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)
headers[header] = value
```

findings.title: Removing xlinkhref from the URL check un-validates it, not removes it
findings.body:
The stated intent is to "drop rarely used SVG attributes we do not need". But this branch is not an allowlist of permitted attributes — it is the dispatch into `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, the scheme check against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). Dropping `xlinkhref` from the condition means `xlink:href` no longer enters that branch and instead falls through to whatever the function's default return is. If the default is permissive (as is typical for an attribute filter that only special-cases URL-bearing attributes), author markdown such as `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` now reaches the DOM unchecked.

Per the module header, this markdown includes end-user-submitted content and `validateProp` is the only barrier, so this is a reachable stored-XSS path rather than a theoretical one. `xlink:href` is a live navigation vector in SVG and is a well-known sanitiser bypass precisely because it is often forgotten.

If the goal is genuinely to stop supporting `xlink:href`, the attribute must be rejected (return `false`) rather than removed from the validated set. Otherwise restore it to the condition.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from client-supplied Content-Length before reading body
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the pooled read-writer from the declared length of the request rather than from bytes actually received. In `cmd/serve/s3`, `contentLength` for an UploadPart request originates from the HTTP `Content-Length` header, which the client controls independently of what it actually sends. A caller can issue `PUT /bucket/key?partNumber=1&uploadId=...` with `Content-Length: 10000000000` and then send a handful of bytes (or stall), and the server commits the memory up front; repeating this across concurrent connections exhausts RAM with negligible attacker cost. Before this change the RW grew page by page as the body was read, so memory tracked real data.

Fix options: cap the reservation at a sane maximum (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)`) and let the RW grow beyond that only as real bytes arrive, and reject or ignore non-positive `contentLength` (chunked/unknown-length requests typically yield -1) rather than passing it through to `Reserve`.

I could not see the `Reserve` implementation or the handler that supplies `contentLength`, so the exact allocation semantics (eager alloc vs. lazy hint) and any upstream size validation are unverified — please confirm both before dismissing.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length

If contentLength is attacker-supplied (as the eval name 'cve-rclone-declared-length-allocation' implies) and does not match the actual body size, or is very large, this now causes an eager allocation of that size. No test in this diff exercises a mismatched or maliciously large contentLength to confirm the reservation is bounded or that a mismatch between declared and actual length is handled correctly (e.g., truncated body, oversized body, or huge declared length with a small pool cap).

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently changes from https to http
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to plaintext when a caller *explicitly* set `meta["is_secure"] = False`; every other case (key absent, i.e. `.get()` returns `None`) defaulted to `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the missing key as falsy and selects `http`.

Since the overwhelming majority of requests never set `is_secure` at all, this flips the default for essentially all S3 traffic from TLS to cleartext, sending AWS requests (including any signed headers/credentials carried on them) over an unencrypted connection. It also changes behaviour for any explicit falsy-but-not-False value such as `0` or `""`, though that is secondary.

If the goal is a simpler expression, keep the secure default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged) or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests now default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset

findings.body: The old logic defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False. The new logic defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy, meaning requests without an explicit is_secure meta key (or with a falsy-but-not-False value) now silently downgrade to plaintext http instead of https. No test file is present in this diff to exercise download_request with is_secure unset, so this security-relevant behavior change would pass unnoticed if wrong.

findings.title: S3 scheme selection logic inverted with different semantics
findings.body: The refactored ternary inverts the logic in a way that changes behavior for the default case. The original code explicitly checked `is_secure is False` to select HTTP, meaning HTTP was only chosen when `is_secure` was explicitly set to False. Any other value (True, None, or missing) defaulted to HTTPS. The new code reverses this: it selects HTTPS only when `is_secure` is truthy, and HTTP for any falsy value including None or missing key. This changes the default scheme from HTTPS to HTTP when the `is_secure` key is absent from request.meta, which is likely the common case. If this handler was documented or designed to default to HTTPS for security, this inverts that contract.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorised as "push", delete action never emitted
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct `"delete"` action. The collapsed form only distinguishes GET/HEAD from everything else, so a DELETE request now produces `Action: "push"`. Any account granted push (e.g. a CI publisher allowed to upload new tags) can now delete existing repositories/manifests, and conversely an account granted only `delete` will be denied. The `ActionDelete` value documented in pkg/api/config/config.go becomes unreachable, so policies written against it silently stop being enforced. Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: DELETE method now maps to 'push', contradicting config documentation
findings.body: The diff removes the case that mapped `http.MethodDelete` to `action = "delete"`. All non-GET/HEAD methods now map to "push", including DELETE. This breaks the contract documented in `pkg/api/config/config.go`, which states that ActionDelete is a distinct action and that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." Since DELETE requests now trigger the 'push' action, the permission model is silently changed: deletion permissions are no longer distinct from push permissions. A caller reading the documented three-action model would be wrong about whether their 'push' permission grants deletion ability.

findings.title: Default for unlisted methods flipped from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm assigned `"pull"` to any method not explicitly listed (OPTIONS, TRACE, custom verbs). The new condition treats every non-GET/HEAD method as `"push"`, so e.g. an OPTIONS/CORS preflight or any unexpected verb now requires push access and will be rejected with 403 for read-only accounts that previously succeeded. If the intent is "reads pull, writes push", enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than inverting the read test.

findings.title: No test verifies DELETE now maps to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The change removes the distinct 'delete' action for HTTP DELETE requests, folding it into 'push'. This is a meaningful authorization-mapping change (per the repo's own docs, delete is intentionally distinct from push) but no test file is part of this diff. If this mapping is wrong or reverted incorrectly, nothing in the given change would catch it.

findings.title: Size guard clears the entire cache, including the entry just written
findings.body: When `_CACHE` crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` drops every cached tenant rather than evicting one. Two consequences: (1) the write on line 10 is immediately undone, so the call that triggered the flush leaves the cache with no record of the tenant it just fetched; (2) every subsequent `get_tenant(...)` returns `None` until callers re-populate, which on a hot path is a cache stampede against `_fetch`. If the intent is a bounded cache, evict a single entry (e.g. `_CACHE.pop(next(iter(_CACHE)))`) or use an LRU (`functools.lru_cache` / `collections.OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) instead of a full flush.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tenant_id can flush the whole shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` unconditionally inserts `tenant_id` into the module-level `_CACHE` (line 10) before any existence/authorisation check on the id, and when the cache exceeds 1000 entries it calls `_CACHE.clear()` (lines 11-12), discarding every other tenant's entry rather than evicting the offending one.

If `tenant_id` is reachable from a request parameter, a caller can loop over 1001 arbitrary ids and force a full cache wipe, sending every subsequent `get_tenant` miss back to `_fetch` — a small amount of attacker work degrades the backing store for all tenants, and repeating it keeps the cache permanently cold. Caching the result of `_fetch` for ids the caller has no right to also means those objects are subsequently served by `get_tenant`, which performs no lookup-time check.

Suggested fixes: bound the cache with a real eviction policy (e.g. an LRU with `maxsize`) instead of `clear()`, and do not insert entries for ids that `_fetch` cannot resolve or that the caller is not entitled to.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage
findings.body: The new function fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared cache, and clears the cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug in the cache-write logic, the eviction condition (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison), or the return value would not be caught.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag with old name
findings.body:
Line 7 of README.md still refers to `--workers`, but the code now uses `--concurrency`. Users reading the documentation will try to use the wrong flag name and their commands will fail. Update the documentation to match the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Flag rename changes args.workers to args.concurrency with no alias
findings.body: Renaming the option also renames argparse's destination attribute: any consumer doing `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError`, and any existing script or CI job passing `--workers` will fail with an unrecognized-argument error. If the intent is purely to align the public flag with the internal name, consider keeping compatibility — e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4, dest="concurrency")` — and/or confirm every `args.workers` read in the codebase has been updated in this PR (none appear in the diff).

findings.title: Flag rename from --workers to --concurrency is untested
findings.body: The argument name changed from --workers to --concurrency, but no test asserts the parser exposes --concurrency (or rejects --workers). If any other code path still references args.workers, or if a caller still passes --workers on the command line, nothing here would fail — the change would silently break CLI usage until observed manually.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function 'Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to counts. Any caller relying on the documented contract will receive an unexpected type and break. Update the docstring to reflect the new return format.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without updating contract
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (e.g. `if monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `total + monthly_usage(a)`) will now raise `TypeError` or silently compare a dict. The docstring on line 2 still claims "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so callers reading it will be misled.

Either keep the function returning the total and add a new `monthly_usage_by_day` for the breakdown, or update every caller and the docstring together.

findings.title: No test verifies the new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. If the query, grouping, or dict construction were wrong (e.g. wrong key names, wrong aggregation, or SQL error), nothing would catch it. Add a test asserting the returned dict's structure and values against known call rows.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter `page_size`
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 documents a parameter called `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 now names it `limit`. This stale documentation will mislead callers about the correct parameter name to use. Update line 6 to read `limit: how many invoices to return.`

findings.title: Renaming keyword parameter page_size breaks keyword callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` is a module-level (non-underscore) function, so its parameter names are part of its callable contract. Any existing call site written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime — this fails only when that path executes, not at import, so it can escape tests. No callers were included in the retrieved context, so the breakage cannot be confirmed or ruled out from what is shown here.

Either grep for `page_size=` at every call site and update them in this same change, or accept the old name for a deprecation window, e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping `page_size` onto `limit` with a warning.

findings.title: Parameter rename has no test verifying the new signature/kwarg usage
findings.body: The function's parameter name changed from page_size to limit (list_invoices signature and the call to _query). If any caller invokes list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=...) as a keyword argument, it will now raise a TypeError, but no test in this diff exercises the function with keyword arguments to catch that break. There's no visible test file in this change or repository context confirming existing coverage for this function.

findings.title: Absolute import of `adapters` will fail at import time
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on `sys.path`. Every other import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` when `requests.sessions` is imported, i.e. the whole package fails to import. Change to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: `verify` and `cert` are accepted but silently dropped on the new request path
findings.body:
The new `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but the body never reads them: it copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto `req`, calls `req.prepare()`, and hands the result to `self.send(prep)`. `send()` in turn builds a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no TLS arguments at all, so neither the per-call value nor any session-level default can reach the connection layer.

The consequence is that a caller writing `session.get(url, verify='/path/to/ca.pem')` or `verify=True` gets whatever the adapter happens to default to, with no error and no warning — if that default is anything other than full verification, every HTTPS call on this path is open to an active network attacker (MITM), and `cert`-based client authentication simply does not happen. A silently ignored security parameter is worse than an unsupported one, because callers believe the control is on.

Either thread `verify`/`cert` through to `adapter.send(...)` (merging with session defaults) or remove them from the signature until the adapter supports them, so the failure is loud.

findings.title: `old_request` calls `_send_request`, which this diff deletes
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper is removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores most of its parameters and all session state
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `return_response` and `config` are accepted and then dropped on the floor. Equally, none of the session-level state is merged in any more: `self.headers`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.cookies`, `self.hooks`, `self.verify`, `self.cert` and `self.config` are never consulted, so a configured `Session` behaves like a bare one. Callers passing `timeout=` or `verify=False` get no error and no effect — a silently wrong result rather than a failure. Either merge session defaults and forward the transport options to `send()`, or raise `NotImplementedError` for the options that are not wired up yet.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send destroys pooling; close() is now a no-op
findings.body: `send()` constructs a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request gets its own connection pool that is discarded (and never closed) afterwards — connection reuse, the whole point of a `Session`, is gone, and sockets are left to the GC. At the same time `close()` was reduced to `pass`, so `with Session() as s:` and explicit `s.close()` no longer release anything. Note also that the adapter is built with no arguments, so `pool_connections`, `pool_maxsize` and `support_http0.9` from `self.config` (previously fed into `init_poolmanager`) are now ignored. The adapter should be created once per Session (e.g. in `__init__`/a mount map) and `close()` should delegate to it.

findings.title: Session.send now delegates to HTTPAdapter with no test covering it
findings.body: Session.send previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs an HTTPAdapter and delegates to adapter.send(request). This is a behavior change to the core send path used by every request, but no test in this diff exercises it. If HTTPAdapter.send has the wrong signature, drops kwargs, or mishandles the request/response, nothing would fail.

findings.title: `self.poolmanager` and `init_poolmanager()` removed; external users may still rely on them
findings.body: `__init__` no longer sets `self.poolmanager`, and the `init_poolmanager()` hook is gone. Both were part of the documented extension surface (subclasses override `init_poolmanager` to customise SSL/pool behaviour) and other modules in this package historically reach for `session.poolmanager` when sending. Any remaining reference — including anything listed in `__attrs__` and pickled via `__getstate__` on line 370 — will now raise `AttributeError` or silently pickle `None`. Please grep for `poolmanager` and `init_poolmanager` across the package and tests before landing. The now-unused `PoolManager` import on line 19 is a hint that this removal was not followed through.

findings.title: close() silently made a no-op, no test would catch resource leak
findings.body: close() previously cleared the poolmanager to release pooled connections; it now just does `pass`. Since poolmanager management moved off Session, this may be intentional, but as written it silently drops all functionality with no test verifying that connections are still released somewhere (e.g. via the adapter) or that close() do anything meaningful.

findings.title: Removed docstring describes stale behavior
findings.body: The `close()` method docstring (lines 131-135 in the original) documented that it disposes of internal state by closing the PoolManager's pooled connections. The implementation has changed to `pass`, making the old docstring now incorrect. Either update the docstring to reflect the new no-op behavior, or remove it entirely if `close()` is now intended to do nothing.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import ...` can resolve to an attacker-placed module
findings.body:
Every other import in this file is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`), but this one is `from adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Under absolute-import semantics this resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so whichever `adapters.py` is found first — including one sitting in the process's working directory or any writable `sys.path` entry — is imported and its `HTTPAdapter` becomes the object that executes every outgoing request. That turns a directory-write primitive into code execution inside the HTTP client.

Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to match the rest of the module and pin resolution to the package.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes `request.cookies` return None
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises on a malformed header, the property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Every caller then fails: `get_cookie` executes `name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` executes `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError`. Since the header is fully attacker-controlled, any client can send `Cookie: garbage` and turn a request into a 500. The previous code never returned a non-mapping (it called `clear_all_cookies()` and still returned a `SimpleCookie`). Reset to an empty jar instead: `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all cookie reads

findings.title: cookies property docstring omits None return on parse failure
findings.body: The `cookies` property docstring states it returns 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects', but the implementation can return `None` when cookie parsing fails (line 523). A caller following the docstring would assume they can safely call dict-like methods on the return value, causing an AttributeError if parsing failed. The docstring must document that `None` is returned on invalid cookies.

findings.title: Public `RequestHandler.cookies` property removed without a delegating shim
No test covers the changed cookie-parse-failure behavior
findings.body: The `cookies` property moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its exception handler changed semantics: previously (in web.py) a parse failure called `self.clear_all_cookies()`; now it sets `self._cookies = None`. Downstream, `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` — both will raise if `cookies` is None. No test exercises a malformed 'Cookie' header to catch this regression, and no test exists for the new property location on HTTPRequest at all.

findings.title: Failed cookie parse no longer triggers clear_all_cookies
findings.body: The old property called `self.clear_all_cookies()` when parsing failed, so a client sending a corrupt Cookie header got Set-Cookie expiry headers back and recovered on the next request. The new property silently swallows the failure and returns a sentinel, so a client stuck with a malformed cookie jar stays stuck. If dropping that behaviour is intentional it is worth noting in the commit message; otherwise restore the clearing at the handler level.

findings.title: Parameter names aren't stripped, so `boundary=` never matches
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX`). `field.partition("=")` then yields `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` test, the loop falls through to the `for ... else` branch, and the request is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" with `self._request.files`/`arguments` left empty. The previous code used a substring search (`'boundary=' in content_type`) and was immune to surrounding whitespace, so this is a regression that silently breaks all normal file uploads. Use `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider stripping `v` / surrounding quotes as well).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Parameter not stripped: ' boundary' never equals 'boundary'

findings.title: No test exercises multipart boundary parsing with leading/non-last params
findings.body: The change alters how the boundary parameter is extracted from a multipart Content-Type header (now scanning all ';'-separated fields instead of assuming boundary is last). No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type header where boundary is not the last parameter (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=utf-8' vs 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=X'), so a regression that reintroduces the old assumption—or breaks parsing when boundary appears first—would not be caught.

findings.title: get_host ignores '?' and '#', allowing host confusion vs. real URL parsers
findings.body:
`get_host` strips the scheme, then only truncates the authority at the first `/`. Query and fragment delimiters are never considered, so for `http://trusted.example?@attacker.example` there is no `/`, the `@` split on line 94-95 discards `trusted.example?` and the function returns host `attacker.example`. The same happens with `http://trusted.example#@attacker.example`. `urllib.parse.urlsplit` returns `trusted.example` for both.

This matters because `get_host` is what urllib3 uses to decide which host to connect to. Any caller that validates a user-supplied URL with a standards-compliant parser (an SSRF allowlist, a "only fetch from our CDN" check, a redirect-target check) and then hands the same string to urllib3 will validate one host and connect to another.

Fix: cut the authority at the first occurrence of any of `/`, `?`, `#` before doing the `@` and `:` splits, e.g. split on a delimiter set rather than `'/'` alone — or delegate to `urlsplit` and only keep the simplified handling for the scheme-less case.

Note this is moved code, not newly written logic, so it may be pre-existing behaviour; I did not see the callers in the provided context.

findings.title: is_connection_dropped raises or returns non-bool for unset conn.sock
findings.body:
`conn.sock` is `None` on an `HTTPConnection` that has not connected yet (and may be absent entirely on non-httplib connection objects). Both branches dereference it unconditionally: `select([None], [], [], 0.0)` raises `TypeError: argument must be an int, or have a fileno() method`, and `p.register(None, POLLIN)` raises the same. If a pool ever checks a freshly-constructed-but-unconnected connection for liveness, this predicate explodes instead of answering.

Also note the return shapes disagree with the docstring's "Returns True": the `select` branch returns a *list* (line 117), the poll branch returns `True` or falls off the end returning `None` (lines 122-125). Callers doing `is_connection_dropped(c) is True` would break. Guard the socket and normalise to bool, e.g.:

```
sock = getattr(conn, 'sock', False)
if sock is False:   # platform-specific: AppEngine
    return False
if sock is None:    # connection already closed
    return True
...
return bool(select([sock], [], [], 0.0)[0])
```

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates the URL, so the exception a caller sees is the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` — the one piece of diagnostic information the error exists to carry is lost. Use `"Failed to parse: %s" % url` (or the original full url captured before the splits, which is more useful since `url` has already been chopped down to the host part by line 97).

findings.title: make_headers silently discards non-str/non-list accept_encoding values
findings.body: The `else` arm assigns `'gzip,deflate'` to anything that is not a `str` or a `list`. That means a tuple, a set, or (under Python 2, which this module targets — it imports `six` on line 16) a `unicode` accept-encoding string is silently thrown away and replaced with `gzip,deflate`, rather than being used as documented on lines 29-33. The caller gets a header they did not ask for with no error. Consider testing against `six.string_types` and treating any non-string iterable via `','.join`, reserving the `gzip,deflate` default for `accept_encoding is True`.

findings.title: No tests included for newly added util.py helpers
findings.body: make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped are moved/introduced here with non-trivial logic (header formatting branches, URL parsing edge cases, platform-specific poll/select behavior) but no test file is part of this diff. If these functions regress (e.g., the malformed error message '%s' with no interpolation argument at line 100, or an off-by-one in URL splitting), nothing would fail. Since this is a refactor consolidating existing helpers, it's unclear whether tests already exist elsewhere in the repo exercising these exact functions post-move; if not, this coverage gap should be addressed.

findings.title: describe() has no test covering either branch
findings.body: The change relies on TypeScript's discriminated-union narrowing to make the casts redundant, but there is no test in this diff exercising describe() for a click event or a key event. If the narrowing were subtly wrong (e.g. property names mismatched at runtime, or the union shape changes later), nothing would fail.

findings.title: location attribute now stores URL object, not string as documented
findings.body:
The documentation in docs/web_reference.rst states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. However, this change now stores `location` as a `URL` object instead of a string. This breaks the documented contract and will cause `str.startswith()` calls in application code to fail with an AttributeError, since URL objects do not have a `startswith` method.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location type change can silently break redirect allowlist checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `HTTPMove.location` now a URL object, not the original string

findings.title: No test guards location attribute's documented string type
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned a `URL` object instead of the string it was constructed with. Per docs/web_reference.rst, application code relies on `self.location` being the original string and calls `str.startswith` on it. A `URL` object does not have `.startswith`, so any code depending on this documented contract would break — but nothing in this diff (or apparently the existing suite) asserts `self.location`'s type or exercises `.startswith()` on it, so this regression would slip through untested.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait` documents that the waiter "is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was exactly that re-check. With `if`, a single spurious/chunk-boundary wake falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns `b""` because the buffer is still empty and `_eof` is still False.

Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`), so this silently truncates streams at chunk boundaries. Restore the `while` loop, or have `_wait` guarantee it only resolves when the buffer is non-empty or EOF is set before any caller relies on a single wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait can return empty bytes, signalling a false EOF to callers

findings.title: No test covers repeated-wake/no-data behavior of readany
findings.body: The change from `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to `if not self._buffer and not self._eof` alters behavior when `_wait` resolves without new data in the buffer (explicitly documented in the docstring of `_wait` as a case that can happen). With `while`, the loop would re-check and wait again; with `if`, the code proceeds to `_read_nowait(-1)` after a single wake even if the buffer is still empty and EOF hasn't been reached, potentially returning an empty read prematurely. No test in the diff or visible suite exercises this documented multi-wake scenario, so a regression here (spurious empty reads, or an assertion failure only under a specific feeder timing) would not be caught.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module loading on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Python 3 removed implicit relative imports (PEP 328), so this resolves against `sys.path` as a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist — importing `requests.sessions` will raise `ModuleNotFoundError`/`ImportError`, taking down the whole package for any consumer. It is also not the "same module" as before in any environment where a top-level `adapters` happens to be installed, in which case the wrong class is silently bound. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching the neighbouring `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager` on line 6.

findings.title: Unqualified `adapters` import allows sys.path module shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` guarantees the class comes from the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` instead, so the first `adapters.py` found on the path wins — including the script directory or an empty/current-directory entry in `sys.path`. Any actor who can drop an `adapters.py` next to the entry-point script (or into any writable path entry, e.g. a world-writable temp dir added by an embedding app) gets their code imported and executed inside `requests`, and their object becomes the transport used for every request: it controls TLS certificate verification, proxy selection, and sees every request body and header. That is arbitrary code execution plus a silent MITM of all HTTP traffic for the host process.

Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or the fully-qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`), which is not resolvable from an attacker-writable path entry.

findings.title: Removing None guard makes get_cookie raise on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented and implemented to return `None` when a Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (`if self._cookies is None: return None`). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied cookie header into a 500 for any handler that calls `get_cookie` — an attacker-triggerable failure since the header is fully client-controlled.

Either restore the guard, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty dict on parse failure (and update its docstring) so the invariant claimed in the PR description actually holds.

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is not always a mapping. The retrieved `cookies` property in `tornado/httpserver.py` returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, raising `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully controlled by any unauthenticated remote client. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by any handler calling `get_cookie` — including internal callers such as XSRF token retrieval and secure-cookie reads, so a single malformed header turns normal requests into unhandled 500s.

Either restore the `is not None` check here, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping on parse failure (and update its docstring) so the invariant claimed in the PR description actually holds.
